title: New US$12 billion research fund, as researchers go unpaid
content:
Tweet
India’s cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, earlier this month approved a new Research Development and Innovation (RDI) Scheme with funds set aside for this purpose of approximately US$12 billion.
“Aimed at enhancing private sector participation in cutting-edge research, the scheme will offer long-term, low- or nil-interest loans to support transformative projects, especially in sunrise and strategic sectors.
“Key goals include scaling up private R&D, funding high-TRL (Technology Readiness Levels) innovations, supporting the acquisition of critical technologies, and establishing a Deep-Tech Fund of Fund,” the official statement said.
India’s newly established overarching science funding agency , the Anusandhan National Research Foundation (ANRF), will oversee the scheme, with the Department of Science and Technology (DST) serving as the principal agency designated by the government to oversee, implement, and monitor the project.
A two-tier funding model envisages a Special Purpose Fund under ANRF channelling resources to second-level fund managers, which will disburse concessional financing.
“The RDI Scheme is a welcome move to boost private sector participation in R&D, especially in a country like India where most research funding still comes from the public sector. Coupled with ANRF’s efforts to reduce red tape, this could improve the research ecosystem,” said Achal Agrawal, founder of India Research Watch, an initiative dedicated to eliminating malpractice in Indian research, told University World News.
“However, transparency is key. In the past, funding has been marred by favouritism and manipulated metrics. Strict oversight and ethical screening are essential. Prioritising sectors like deep tech, quantum computing, and semiconductors makes sense, but success will depend on how well the scheme is implemented,” he added.
Focus on commercial research
Union Minister of State JitendraSingh, during an event in Delhi in March, announced: “India’s R&D spending has more than doubled in the last decade.”
A closer look reveals that a large portion of the science budget is allocated to interest-free loans for private sector innovation, leaving academic researchers underfunded and unsupported, said a researcher.
Nonetheless, it may lead to collaborative funding with universities and institutions. “We are seeing a very significant growth in industry collaborations, and we are seeing very high growth rates in terms of funding,” Professor Rangan Banerjee, director of the Indian Institute of Technology, Delhi, told University World News recently. But he noted public funding is still significantly higher than industry funding.
Banerjee pointed to more government-industry-university research models for IITs in future. “Industry is increasingly relying on technology development and research; there is a very clear trend in that, so the ecosystem – it still has a long way to go, but it is growing.”
NV Varghese, a distinguished visiting professor at the Indian Institute of Technology, Bombay, and former vice-chancellor of the National Institute of Educational Planning and Administration (NIEPA) in New Delhi, said the funding allocation showed a renewed policy interest in research.
“The real test lies in how effectively the RDI scheme is implemented,” Varghese told University World News.
“So far, the focus seems to be on science and technology, with social sciences and humanities on the margins. A key concern is whether it will genuinely strengthen research in public universities or simply benefit elite institutions.
“India has over 1,300 universities, but fewer than half conduct serious research. Without addressing gaps in funding, infrastructure, and faculty training, we risk deepening existing inequalities. What’s needed is not just money, but a culture of inquiry and institutional capacity across the system,” he said.
Stipend delays causing distress
The government’s funding of industrial research comes amid a deepening crisis in academic research, with many early-career scholars citing delayed funding and institutional apathy, particularly in core disciplines, as major sources of disillusionment.
The ambitions of some of the brightest scholars are being hindered by bureaucratic delays in funding and mismanagement, experts have said, with the situation significantly deteriorating in the past two years. Central to this issue is the INSPIRE (Innovation in Science Pursuit for Inspired Research) Fellowship, a key initiative launched in 2008 by the government’s Department of Science and Technology (DST) aimed at encouraging students to pursue PhDs in basic and applied sciences. While the fellowship is designed to provide monthly stipends ranging from around INR37,000 to 42,000 (US$430 to US$488), ongoing delays in disbursing the funds pushed many researchers into financial and emotional distress. Throughout the country, young researchers – some of whom have ranked in the top 1% in their Standard 12 (school leaving) examinations or excelled in competitive exams like the IIT-JEE for entry to the Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs) – are voicing concerns about stipends delayed by as long as 13 months. Researchers from esteemed institutions such as IITs and Indian Institutes of Science Education and Research (IISERs) expressed frustration over excessive delays. Many of them report that emails to DST go unanswered, and responses from helplines are often indifferent or dismissive. Sayali Atkare, an INSPIRE senior researcher at the Savitribai Phule Pune University, said in a LinkedIn post: “For over a year now, many of us who are pursuing PhDs under DST-funded fellowships have not received our stipends. That’s 13+ (in some cases 18+) months without financial support, despite contributing to the scientific and academic progress of this nation.” Additionally, the funding imbalance fosters inequity within the research community, according to many researchers interviewed. Students from privileged backgrounds are better able to withstand delays through family support or personal savings. In contrast, scholars from lower-income households face the difficult choice between continuing their research and meeting basic living expenses – a dilemma no aspiring scientist should have to confront, added the researchers. Many academics have expressed that the consequences of these funding delays reach far beyond individual struggles. At several central universities, researchers have reported being unable to attend conferences due to delayed fellowships. Agrawal said such funding delays were deeply concerning. “INSPIRE is one of the most prestigious fellowships awarded to select students, and if they have to struggle even for basic financial support, it sends a discouraging message to future PhD aspirants. It could very well make students think twice before pursuing a PhD in India.” He called for the issue to be quickly resolved and hoped “more effective systems are put in place to ensure timely disbursal of fellowships." Time lags are common The delays are not new; many scholars have come to anticipate a three-to-four-month lag in receiving payments, which they reluctantly incorporate into their annual planning. However, the situation has become worse. The issues arise from changes in fund management at the Department of Science and Technology (DST), including the introduction of zero-balance accounts, which do not require a minimum balance, and revised accounting systems. Although these reforms aim to enhance transparency, they have resulted in confusion and disorganisation, making it difficult for people to understand procedures or carry out tasks effectively. Scholars, who depend on these fellowships for their living expenses, research materials, and academic tools, say they are facing the consequnces. A researcher currently pursuing a PhD from India’s Defence Research and Development Organisation’s Defence Research & Development Establishment (DRDE), which specialises in detection of and protection against hazardous chemical and biological agents, outlined her frustration with the financial instability. “Since it’s a defence organisation, we must follow strict protocols. Everything was fine until DST asked us to open a new account in the Bank of Maharashtra. It took over a year for DRDE to open it, that too by bypassing usual procedures,” she said, requesting anonymity. “During my third year, we faced extreme financial stress – just when we needed to focus on our research.” Although her fellowship for the next year was approved in September 2024, no funds have been released. “DST said they lacked funds. It’s been one and a half years without fellowship (money), despite multiple emails and phone calls,” she added. In response to mounting pressure and widespread social media campaigns where scholars have tagged Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Minister of State for Science and Technology Jitendra Singh – there has been no official communication so far. When contacted on the issue, DST Secretary Professor Abhay Karandikar did not respond. Earlier in May, Abhay Karandikar told The Hindu newspaper that starting from June 2025, all pending dues would be cleared, and scholars would begin receiving their funds on time.

“The real test lies in how effectively the RDI scheme is implemented,” Varghese told University World News.
“So far, the focus seems to be on science and technology, with social sciences and humanities on the margins. A key concern is whether it will genuinely strengthen research in public universities or simply benefit elite institutions.
“India has over 1,300 universities, but fewer than half conduct serious research. Without addressing gaps in funding, infrastructure, and faculty training, we risk deepening existing inequalities. What’s needed is not just money, but a culture of inquiry and institutional capacity across the system,” he said.
Stipend delays causing distress
The government’s funding of industrial research comes amid a deepening crisis in academic research, with many early-career scholars citing delayed funding and institutional apathy, particularly in core disciplines, as major sources of disillusionment.
The ambitions of some of the brightest scholars are being hindered by bureaucratic delays in funding and mismanagement, experts have said, with the situation significantly deteriorating in the past two years. Central to this issue is the INSPIRE (Innovation in Science Pursuit for Inspired Research) Fellowship, a key initiative launched in 2008 by the government’s Department of Science and Technology (DST) aimed at encouraging students to pursue PhDs in basic and applied sciences. While the fellowship is designed to provide monthly stipends ranging from around INR37,000 to 42,000 (US$430 to US$488), ongoing delays in disbursing the funds pushed many researchers into financial and emotional distress. Throughout the country, young researchers – some of whom have ranked in the top 1% in their Standard 12 (school leaving) examinations or excelled in competitive exams like the IIT-JEE for entry to the Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs) – are voicing concerns about stipends delayed by as long as 13 months. Researchers from esteemed institutions such as IITs and Indian Institutes of Science Education and Research (IISERs) expressed frustration over excessive delays. Many of them report that emails to DST go unanswered, and responses from helplines are often indifferent or dismissive. Sayali Atkare, an INSPIRE senior researcher at the Savitribai Phule Pune University, said in a LinkedIn post: “For over a year now, many of us who are pursuing PhDs under DST-funded fellowships have not received our stipends. That’s 13+ (in some cases 18+) months without financial support, despite contributing to the scientific and academic progress of this nation.” Additionally, the funding imbalance fosters inequity within the research community, according to many researchers interviewed. Students from privileged backgrounds are better able to withstand delays through family support or personal savings. In contrast, scholars from lower-income households face the difficult choice between continuing their research and meeting basic living expenses – a dilemma no aspiring scientist should have to confront, added the researchers. Many academics have expressed that the consequences of these funding delays reach far beyond individual struggles. At several central universities, researchers have reported being unable to attend conferences due to delayed fellowships. Agrawal said such funding delays were deeply concerning. “INSPIRE is one of the most prestigious fellowships awarded to select students, and if they have to struggle even for basic financial support, it sends a discouraging message to future PhD aspirants. It could very well make students think twice before pursuing a PhD in India.” He called for the issue to be quickly resolved and hoped “more effective systems are put in place to ensure timely disbursal of fellowships." Time lags are common The delays are not new; many scholars have come to anticipate a three-to-four-month lag in receiving payments, which they reluctantly incorporate into their annual planning. However, the situation has become worse. The issues arise from changes in fund management at the Department of Science and Technology (DST), including the introduction of zero-balance accounts, which do not require a minimum balance, and revised accounting systems. Although these reforms aim to enhance transparency, they have resulted in confusion and disorganisation, making it difficult for people to understand procedures or carry out tasks effectively. Scholars, who depend on these fellowships for their living expenses, research materials, and academic tools, say they are facing the consequnces. A researcher currently pursuing a PhD from India’s Defence Research and Development Organisation’s Defence Research & Development Establishment (DRDE), which specialises in detection of and protection against hazardous chemical and biological agents, outlined her frustration with the financial instability. “Since it’s a defence organisation, we must follow strict protocols. Everything was fine until DST asked us to open a new account in the Bank of Maharashtra. It took over a year for DRDE to open it, that too by bypassing usual procedures,” she said, requesting anonymity. “During my third year, we faced extreme financial stress – just when we needed to focus on our research.” Although her fellowship for the next year was approved in September 2024, no funds have been released. “DST said they lacked funds. It’s been one and a half years without fellowship (money), despite multiple emails and phone calls,” she added. In response to mounting pressure and widespread social media campaigns where scholars have tagged Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Minister of State for Science and Technology Jitendra Singh – there has been no official communication so far. When contacted on the issue, DST Secretary Professor Abhay Karandikar did not respond. Earlier in May, Abhay Karandikar told The Hindu newspaper that starting from June 2025, all pending dues would be cleared, and scholars would begin receiving their funds on time.

title: Medical schools face challenges as boycotting students return
content:
Tweet
Medical students in South Korea have said they will return to their university courses after an extended boycott that lasted almost a year and a half. However, student groups have not specified when or how the return would take place, while medical schools face considerable hurdles organising the education of different cohorts after so many months of disruption.
The Korean Medical Students Association (KMSA) issued a joint statement alongside the Korean Medical Association (KMA) and the chairs of the Education and Health and Welfare Committees of the National Assembly during a press conference at KMA headquarters in Yongsan, Seoul, on 12 July.
“By trusting in the government and the National Assembly, all students will return to school and do their utmost to normalise medical education and the healthcare system,” the statement said.
Students called on President Lee’s administration to restore academic schedules and create pathways for them to return.
The announcement marks the first collective declaration to return in 17 months, after the mass leave of absence that began in February 2024 in protest against the government’s policy to expand medical school enrolment by an extra 2,000 places. The protests escalated when medical school professors resigned in solidarity with medical students and junior doctors, leaving the country’s medical education and training in a deep, prolonged crisis.
The declaration to return came as the new president, Lee Jae-Myung, was elected last month, replacing former president Yoon Suk-yeol, who was impeached for his role in imposing martial law last December.
The joint statement called for the formation of a consultative body to address the damage to the country’s healthcare system caused by what they described as the “reckless” policies of the previous administration.
President Lee Jae-Myung welcomed the students’ declaration. Speaking at a 15 July cabinet meeting at the presidential office, he said “It is belated, but a truly fortunate development,” and instructed education authorities to “swiftly take all necessary follow-up measures.”
Lee also stressed the need for better communication with healthcare professionals – some believe this was one of the reasons behind the protracted crisis. “Communication is always important, but in our society, there is far too little of it,” the president remarked.
“It’s not about blaming any particular side, but I hope that from now on, meaningful dialogue can take place across all areas. I ask our officials to maintain close communication with medical personnel,”  Lee said.
Addressing the returning students directly, he said “As future healthcare professionals entrusted with the public’s health and lives, please reflect more deeply on the meaning of your social responsibilities.”
Unresolved issues
With many medical schools set to finalise academic penalties for boycotting students by late July, some analysts see the timing of the return announcement as a tactic to pressure the government into enabling re-enrolment before decisions on failing students and expulsions are locked in.
Most medical students who boycotted classes for an extended period have violated their universities’ academic regulations. Strictly enforced academic credit requirements mean that exceeding a certain threshold of absence can lead to students being held back or even expelled.
However, the practicalities and procedures to be followed and whether the return of so many students is even possible – remain unresolved.
Welcoming the announcement, the Education Ministry said in a statement on Saturday: “When it comes to the timing and method of their return, we need to conduct sufficient discussions and review individual universities’ academic schedules with the relevant ministries, (as well as) educational conditions and curricular specifics.”
A small number of students – particularly third- and fourth-year clinical students – returned earlier this year, for practical training, but most students stayed away throughout the first semester of this year, between March and June.
Adjusting to several cohorts Recognising the scale of the problem of overlapping cohorts, the KMSA, National Assembly members, and KMA jointly urged the government to devise a comprehensive strategy to allow medical students to resume their education. According to university academic regulations, some 8,300 students across all academic years – over 40% of the country’s medical students – could be held back a year, while 46 students are at risk of expulsion, according to figures compiled by the Ministry of Education on 9 May, following a survey of all 40 medical schools nationwide. This has significant implications for medical education across the country. If all affected students from the 2024, 2025, and 2026 cohorts are able to continue their studies, they will have to take classes concurrently during the same academic year. South Korea’s medical education and training programmes are structured on a year-round basis rather than a semester system. Even if students admitted in 2024 return this July, they cannot start to make up missed coursework until the next academic year. While first- and second-year students – who primarily take general education modules – could potentially catch up during the summer break and the second semester, third- and fourth-year students are required to complete more than 40 weeks of specialised coursework each year, making the organisation of make-up sessions particularly difficult. Students in their final years must also complete clinical training to qualify for the national medical licensing exam, a requirement unlikely to be met even if the students are reinstated immediately. Frictions between students Another emerging concern is possible friction between students who returned earlier and those who remained on strike. During the prolonged walkout, students who re-enrolled early were often subjected to criticism or even ridicule from their peers. A third-year student who returned to a national university in March this year admitted some apprehension. “Some of my seniors are only returning now. If we end up studying together during clinical rotations, I’m honestly afraid they might bully or ostracise me because I returned before them,” the student told University World News. A professor at a university in the capital region, who is a member of the Korean Association of Medical Colleges, told University World News: “there is discussion on whether to require returning students to sign a pledge respecting the learning rights of those who returned earlier”. President’s response At the cabinet meeting this week, President Lee directed relevant departments to carefully review and address the shortages in public healthcare, essential services, and emergency medicine. Lee Sun-woo, emergency response committee chair of the KMSA, said in a statement following the cabinet meeting that the disruption in the healthcare sector was due to the previous government’s abrupt implementation of policy. He said: “It is our hope that a culture of consensus and proper procedures will take root so that such incidents are never repeated.” The joint declaration demanded guaranteed participation from medical students in future discussions concerning medium- and long-term improvements to the education and training environment.

title: Polar research sheds light on climate impact in tropics
content:
Tweet
Thailand, which is not typically thought of as a ‘polar’ country, is seeing a boom in polar science. According to Thai specialists, researching the polar regions has significant ramifications for tropical coastal and environmental resilience as well as the effects of climate change.
Some critics in Thailand question why Thai scientists need to do research in remote and icy locations in the Antarctic, over 11,000 km away from tropical Thailand, which is located close to the equator.
However, Professor Suchana Chavanich of the Department of Marine Science at Chulalongkorn University, Bangkok, described research in the Arctic and Antarctic as “a kind of frontier research”.
“What we learnt from that (Arctic research) is that when the sea ice melts, it does not just have an impact in the polar regions but could have an impact on a tropical country like Thailand,” she told University World News.
“In the past 10 years, we see more coastal erosion occurring in Thailand. Not only that, but we see more frequent flooding along the coastline, and that is not just because of climate change but because of the sea level rise. Now we know the problem occurs because of sea ice melting,” she noted.
“Many scientists from other countries want to go there (to polar regions) as well, because we cannot see the real impacts if we stay in our own countries in the tropics,” she added.
Chavanich pointed out that polar regions are the carbon sinks of the world. Carbon dioxide emissions are “blown away” by prevailing winds and the earth’s rotations towards the poles and melt the ice there.
“The majority of carbon dioxide is now accumulated in those two (polar) areas, and because of the high accumulation, it has caused tremendous effects on those two regions,” she said.
“We cannot say that this matter is irrelevant to us or that the Poles are too far away,” she noted , saying it is important for people in Thailand to be aware of the extent of global warming and help change lifestyles to reduce gas emissions to the atmosphere.
Chavanich has previously said that participation in Thailand’s Polar Research Project, under a royal initiative of Thai Princess Royal Maha Chakri Sirindhorm, “shows that Thailand gives high priority to global warming, which is a worldwide problem.
A study by a team of Thai researchers will be like a piece of the jigsaw puzzle that, when combined with research from other countries, will provide us with a bigger picture of the situation’s impact on the world at the moment. This will be beneficial in preparing ourselves for the impending climate change”.
Collaboration with China
Thai scientists are collaborating with China, which considers itself a ‘near-Arctic state’ despite its distance from the Arctic circle and is one of five Asian countries that are permanent observers to the intergovernmental Arctic Council, participating in some council activities and contributing to scientific research. Other Asian countries are India, Japan, Singapore, and South Korea.
Meanwhile, the Antarctic Treaty that came into force in 1961 now has 58 member countries. Since Thailand is not a signatory to the treaty, it had to partner with a treaty member – China – to take part in research in the southern polar region.
In the north, China has research bases in the Norwegian archipelago of Svalbard and the China-Iceland Arctic Observatory in northern Iceland. In the south, it has five research stations in Antarctica. China operates four icebreaker research vessels to support these research stations.
“By going there and working with the Chinese and other international scientists, we have gained valuable scientific knowledge to raise awareness in Thailand (about the impact of melting ice) on the rising sea levels here,” Chavanich said,
China’s Antarctic research stations are supported by its research vessel Xue Long 2, its 13,990 tonne-jewel in the crown of polar research exploration, notable for its ability to break ice both forward and backward, navigating through ice up to 1.5 meters thick.
Xue Long 2 most recently docked at Chonburi Pier near Bangkok in May, coinciding with an international scientific symposium on polar research held at Bangkok’s Chulalongkorn University, jointly organised by the university, the Polar Science Consortium of Thailand (PSCT), and the Polar Research Institute of China (PRIC).
Sun Shuxian, China’s vice-minister of Natural Resources, addressing the Bangkok symposium, warned that ice was melting at an alarming velocity in the Arctic, and this phenomenon needed urgent international scrutiny and committed action in order to limit it.
“The Arctic’s icy heart is melting away,” he said in an impassioned plea. “It is imperative that our nations unite against this warming world. “Our collaboration (with Thailand) continues to expand into new frontiers, with joint research now prioritising polar environmental changes and global impacts, atmospheric sciences, oceanographic studies, and astronomical observations,” he noted. Work at Chinese research stations The collaboration between China and Thailand began in 2013 when Thai Princess Royal Maha Chakri Sirindhorn envisaged Thai scientists making a foray into polar research with international partners, including China. By 2016, this was crystallised with an MOU signed between China’s Arctic and Antarctic Administration and a coalition of five Thai universities, including Chulalongkorn, Burapha University, the National Institute of Development Administration, the National Astronomical Research Institute of Thailand, and the Thailand National Science and Technology Development Agency. The princess was the first person from Thailand to visit Antarctica in November 1993 to observe research conducted at New Zealand’s Scott Base. She initiated the Polar Research Project, setting up the Polar Research Team of Thailand, which has sent 19 Thai scientists to Antarctica and 15 to the Arctic to conduct research on climate change and other issues. Thai-China research efforts are led by two female marine scientists from Chulalongkorn University. In 2013, Chavanich became the first diver at the 30-year-old Chinese research station to dive into the icy waters to observe marine life around the station. As it was a dangerous undertaking, China had assistance from South Korean and Chilean missions close by to help monitor the dive. Chavanich’s colleague at Chulalongkorn’s Marine Science Department, Assistant Professor Sujaree Bureekul, pointed to the challenges of doing research at the frigid North Pole. “Every icy gust taught me anew,” Bureekul told the May symposium, reflecting on her experience conducting water sampling, sea ice monitoring, and volcanism studies in the Arctic. “These experiences broadened my perspective on polar systems and multidisciplinary science,” she said. She added: “the Arctic holds keys to mysteries yet to unfold.” Bureekul, who joined a previous Xue Long 2 research expedition to the Arctic in 2023, told China Daily: “without such collaboration with China, we would never be able to do such remarkable polar trips, which allow us to have firsthand information about the icy continents”. The Thai scientists’ most recent trip to the South Pole was in January this year, when Chavanich joined the Chinese Antarctic expedition team along with Bureekul and Nipat Pinpradet, assistant researcher, Department of Marine Science, Burapha University, staying at China’s Great Wall Station for a month. Microplastics pollution Research by Thai and Chinese scientists in the Antarctic included investigating extremely strong winds and the impacts of global warming, how melting ice led to emerging diseases in marine animals, and declining penguin populations due to disrupted food chains. Another area of research is microplastic pollution. The discovery by researchers of microplastics trapped in sea ice indicated that Antarctica is becoming a global waste sink. Sun told the May symposium that marine pollution, such as the accumulation of microplastics contaminating seawater and the air in the Arctic Ocean, needed to be closely monitored. Another key concern is the link between global warming and emerging infectious diseases. “Global warming affects marine ecosystems. Fish behaviour changes as the ice melts. The water temperature rises, and their eating habits change. They’ve become more insatiable in their hunger and keep eating more and more, resulting in more parasites in their bodies,” said Chavanich. “This indicates that when the earth’s temperature rises, new diseases emerge, that is, an increased number of parasites in fishes. This results in the higher death rate of penguin chicks and seal pups whose survival rate is only at 10%,” she reported after the January-February trip. She added: “The (microplastics) waste that fish eat will stick in the stomach, causing cancer and affecting the growth of the fish.” Noting the growing recognition of polar science in Thailand and its link to coastal and environmental resilience, Chavanich said: “The cooperation promotes capacity building through shared research, exchange programmes, and marine ecosystem studies. “The China-Thailand partnership aims to be a model of international scientific collaboration and address urgent planetary concerns.” Chavanich stressed: “Our journey has just begun; together we can carve pathways to sustainability.”

title: New regulations on distance learning broadly welcomed
content:
Tweet
Brazil’s new regulatory framework for distance learning has been broadly welcomed in the higher education sector.
New legislation setting out to both strengthen the quality of distance education and limit its use in certain programmes was introduced in legislation signed off in May.
It prohibits 100% remote undergraduate courses and ensures that only 30% of the workload of in-person programmes can now include distance learning activities.
The legislation represents a response to concerns about the huge rise in remote learning over the past decade and the impact on the quality of higher education provision.
According to the Ministry of Education, the changes introduced in the decree seek to boost the quality of distance learning in Brazilian higher education while recognising it as a strategic tool for education expansion and access.
Minister of Education Camilo Santana, speaking at the signing ceremony, said: “We believe that distance learning can provide students with an experience as rich as that of other programmes, as long as there is an effective commitment from everyone to the teaching and learning process.”
Claudia Costi, former senior director for global education at the World Bank, said the measures are “positive, even if overdue”.
“Distance learning is certainly a way to expand access to higher education – this has been the case in other countries – but it must be quality education. There’s no point in reaching remote areas if the education offered is poor,” she said, as reported by Valor International.
Costin noted that one in two students drop out of distance learning programmes and poor course quality is a key reason.
The Foundation for the Center for Science and Distance Higher Education of the State of Rio de Janeiro (Cecierj Foundation) told CNN Brazil that the new guidelines will have a positive impact on distance learning and defends this model as an important tool for the democratisation of access to higher education.
Threefold increase in programmes
Enrolments in distance learning programmes in Brazil have grown by 326% in 10 years, reaching 4.91 million students between 2022 and 2023 and representing almost half of the total enrolments in Brazilian higher education.
At the same time, enrolments in the in-person programmes fell by 29.1% between 2013 and 2023, according to the 15th edition of the Map of Brazilian Higher Education.
The new legislation, which was signed into law by President Luís Inácio Lula da Silva on 19 May, is the result of a dialogue across different sectors of Brazilian society about the need for a new Distance Learning Policy and will be regulated by the Ministry of Education and the National Council of Education.
Decree 12546 was drafted by a committee of experts with extensive experience in distance education and public policy.
It also involved meetings with the Advisory Council for the Improvement of Higher Education Regulation and Supervision Processes; technical visits and meetings with representative bodies, social movements, and international experts; as well as public hearings at the Education Committee of the Chamber of Deputies.
Clearer definitions set out
The new decree includes clear definitions of in-person, hybrid, and distance learning programmes.
Hybrid programmes, which are a new format, will include at least 30% in-person activities (professional internships, outreach activities, and laboratory practices), and at least 20% will involve either in-person or facilitated synchronous activities – real-time interactions with a maximum of 70 students per teacher and facilitator and controls on attendance.
Under the new rules in Brazil, distance learning programmes should comprise a minimum of 20% in-person and-or mediated synchronous activities. Each distance learning course will have to include at least one in-person test focused on analysis, synthesis, or practice, which will have the highest weighting of any single element in the final grade. Certain undergraduate programmes have been ruled incompatible with distance learning. They are medicine, law, dentistry, nursing, and psychology. Distance learning is also prohibited in medicine programmes. Other programmes in the field of health and programmes for professional training (“licenciaturas”) can only exist in in-person or hybrid formats. Higher education institutions interested in offering distance learning programmes must request a specific accreditation from the Ministry of Education. One of the new requirements for obtaining this accreditation is that the institution must have a distance learning centre, which must include resources such as internet, study spaces and laboratories (where applicable), and academic spaces that support students. They must also have facilitators – described as ‘teaching mediators’ – and tutors. Tutors must be trained in the courses they will teach. Also, facilitators must only perform administrative tasks and no teaching functions. Changes to be brought in gradually The changes outlined in the decree will be introduced gradually. According to the Ministry of Education, higher education institutions will have two years to adapt their programmes. Students enrolled in distance learning programmes with different characteristics from those covered by the decree will be able to complete their studies with no changes. Since its creation, the decree has received a lot of attention from bodies representing private higher education institutions, which account for 79.3% of total higher education enrolments in Brazil and were responsible for offering 95.9% of distance learning courses in Brazil in 2023. While the new decree imposes limits and requirements as a means to ensure quality, its implementation and how it will be monitored present significant challenges for the Brazilian government in the coming period. Janguiê Diniz, CEO of the Brazilian Association of Higher Education Providers (ABMES), highlighted the essential role that distance education plays in the democratisation of Brazilian higher education and warned of the risks that this could go backwards if the regulation is implemented without dialogue and balance. Distance learning is of paramount importance for Brazil. Many people were only able to reach higher education thanks to it,” Diniz said in a live broadcast on YouTube held a few hours after the publication of the decree. ABMES, which contributed to the formation of the new decree, also held a seminar on 10 June, titled “New distance learning milestone: perspectives, challenges, and paths”. Financial analysts present at the event warned that the decree is likely to increase operational costs for institutions, especially with the requirement for mediated synchronous activities and adaptations in distance learning centres, in addition to reducing revenues through the ending of high-margin distance learning courses such as nursing. In general, the education media agrees that the decree is positive, although some have been critical of the delays in tackling the issue and say the proposals don’t go far enough. Professor Joana Angélica Guimarães da Luz , rector of the Federal University of Southern Bahia, in an article in Folha de São Paulo, complained about a lack of debate about the use of distance learning in Brazilian public universities, which generally offer better teaching and research. She wrote: “With the current technological advances and an ever-increasing network of public universities spread throughout all regions of Brazil, the conditions are already in place for a better-founded public distance education network to exist throughout the Brazilian territory.” Increasingly popular teaching method Distance learning is an increasingly popular teaching method in other South American countries, which has both positives and negatives. On the one hand, it has the potential to expand access to higher education, and on the other, it promotes the privatisation of the system, with risks to the quality of education. Argentina and Paraguay have updated their legislation on distance learning in higher education in recent years, the former in 2023 and the latter in 2024. Both have reduced the use of distance learning as an asynchronous method but make no reference to real-time online interactions. Like Brazil, Paraguay defines some areas in which distance learning is not acceptable. These are natural sciences, engineering and technology, medical sciences and agricultural sciences.

title: Bangladeshi students reject political and media hostility
content:
Tweet
Bangladeshi students have voiced strong concerns over increasingly hostile media coverage by the right-wing press in Denmark, fuelling fears of growing ‘Muslim immigration’ at Denmark’s universities, and claims by right-wing politicians that they are exploiting loopholes in immigration law to take Danish jobs.
The Bangladesh Association of Students and Alumni (BASAD) in Denmark said it is “deeply concerned by the tone and framing” of the coverage on 24NEWS and by the Ritzau news agency of reports of increasing numbers of students coming to Denmark from Bangladesh.
“These students come to Denmark through transparent, lawful processes – meeting all academic and visa requirements, paying high tuition fees, and pursuing their studies in accordance with Danish standards.
“Their presence reflects the strength and credibility of Denmark’s education system, not a flaw in it,” BASAD told University World News.
On 9 July the newspaper Berlingske Tidende ran the headline: “Remarkable increase in students from Bangladesh: It smells like something we’ve seen before”, alluding to the influx of Nepalese students earlier this year as reported by University World News .
“It has been about two months since Minister for Immigration and Integration Kaare Dybvad Bek closed a loophole in the law that gave people from third-world countries direct access to the Danish labour market. Now it appears that a new one has opened, says the union”, the newspaper stated.
This was followed by a report in the Fagbladet 3F with the
headline : “Every sixth student at RUC university [Roskilde masters] is from Bangladesh”.
In 2024, one in six newly admitted masters students at Roskilde University (RUC) was from Bangladesh, the publication said, claiming: “It is most likely that people from Bangladesh use study stays in Denmark as a backdoor to the Danish labour market and permanent residence.”
The report said suspicion had long been simmering that Bangladeshis were gaining easy access to the Danish labour market through study stays at the country’s universities, bypassing the usual rules that regulate employment of international labour.
While nine students from Bangladesh were admitted to RUC in 2020, that number had increased to 300 in 2024 – more than 30 times more, the publication reported.
Denmark’s right-wing parties quickly responded, demanding action. The Danish People’s Party’s immigration spokesperson Mikkel Bjørn, told 24NEWS: “It is deeply serious that Islamic immigration is growing at our universities. We have seen time and time again that so-called temporary presence becomes permanent residence. It starts with a study stay – and ends with family reunification and a lifelong presence.”
On 9 July, Peter Skaarup of the right-wing populist Denmark Democrats party asked the Minister of Immigration and Integration Kaare Dybvad Bek in Parliament to comment on the Berlingske Tidende report and to explain “whether the government is ready to look at measures that close the loophole to the Danish labour market that currently exists for students from third countries on state-approved programmes”.
He demanded detailed information from the minister breaking down the number of immigrants from Bangladesh arriving in 2019-2025 on the basis of their residence category, such as asylum, employment, family reunification, study, or other.
BASAD told University World News that Bangladeshi students were being unfairly characterised as undocumented migrants when in fact they had come through legal channels. “It is especially disappointing to see narratives that misrepresent this community. These students are not exploiting the system – they are fully engaged in it: paying tuition, following legal requirements, and contributing academically and economically,” it said. It was important to highlight that access to the labour market is a standard feature of international student policies globally, BASAD said. “In countries with limited scholarship opportunities, part-time work is often essential not only for financial survival but also for integration and professional growth. This is not a loophole – it is a natural and expected part of the international education experience,” BASAD noted. Some Bangladeshi students have been documenting their compatriots’ study experience in Denmark as part of their research. At Aalborg University, Nusrat Jahan Shimul delivered her MSc in Global Refugee Studies thesis in 2024, which found that Bangladeshi students face unequal treatment not only in the labour market but also within their educational institutions in Denmark. “I am myself a student migrant from Bangladesh pursuing my master’s degree. During my whole study period, I have struggled a lot maintaining the balance between my study, work, and personal life. While searching for jobs, I have been discriminated against because of language and limited working hours as per my immigration rules,” Shimul stated. The Danish Development Research Network Sabbir Irfan reported last year that there had been a surge in Bangladeshi students dropping out of their programmes, which posed a significant challenge for institutions and the Danish education system. This was despite the fact that a “substantial portion” of Bangladeshi students “excel academically and pursue diverse paths post-graduation – such as returning to Bangladesh or relocating to other countries with developmental project works, or settling in Denmark for enhanced opportunities”. Susan Wright, Professor of Educational Anthropology at the Danish School of Education at Aarhus University, told University World News that Denmark is trying to re-internationalise its higher education “but limits its ambition to only attracting international students who will contribute as graduates to the Danish economy”. The viability of a university programme is thus gauged by the number of graduates employed in the Danish labour market. Wright said this poses two problems. First, she said, many Danish as well as international students take courses with the aim of contributing to social and economic development elsewhere in the world, not just in Denmark. “These students might be employed in their home country or in global companies, NGOs, or international organisations and be ambassadors for Denmark and its education. But they do not ‘count’ in the statistics on graduate employment for their university programme, and their absence from the Danish labour market may well undermine the viability of that programme.” Second, as the Bangladeshi Students’ Association makes clear and as is also reflected in research at the Centre for Higher Education Futures , she said that international students face great difficulties in obtaining student jobs, let alone employment after graduation, that relate to their studies and help them build a career in Denmark. She added that many in Denmark think that the kind of prejudice exemplified by the newspaper headlines about this case are damaging Denmark's image. Christoffer Rosenkvist, chair of the National Union of Students in Denmark, told University World News: “The increase in applications from Bangladesh is certainly significant. However, it is very important to note that, within the current Danish legal framework, it is legal for foreign non-EU students to study and work in Denmark provided all conditions here are met. “The internationalisation of our higher educational institutions is not only a huge asset for our students and educational institutions, but for Danish society as a whole,” he said. He added that, when considering solutions to the problems of employment, it is important to address both the study and work conditions of the students in question. Iris Kimizoglu, president of the European Students’ Union, told University World News, that addressing any issue concerning a minority of students misusing visas should not impact the majority of Bangladeshi students who had fulfilled all the legal requirements on entry. “We reject xenophobic and racist narratives and warn against measures that discredit and disadvantage the broad majority of honest students from Bangladesh,” she said. Dr Bernd Parusel, senior researcher in political science at the Swedish Institute for European Policy Studies and an expert on migration, told University World News that reports about international students using their residence permits or visas for reasons other than studying have also been a concern in many other European Union member countries, as a briefing from the European Migration Network showed a couple of years ago. “Governments and higher education institutions are facing a dilemma. On the one hand, they know that allowing international students to work, at least part-time, is important for many students, especially in countries where tuition fees or the cost of living are high. “If a destination country is very strict regarding students’ right to work, that makes the country less attractive as a destination for students,” he stated. “After all, many domestic students work as well. On the other hand, countries want to make sure that those that are admitted for study purposes really have studying as their main intention. Governments also want to avoid exploitation in the labour market and wage-dumping,” he added. He said that solving this dilemma by finding a reasonable middle ground between these two political goals is not easy. “If study permits are used for work purposes, including low-skilled work, that also shows that European countries have a huge demand for foreign labour,” he stated. “Officially, some EU countries only want to attract skilled workers for high-paid jobs, but our economies have a big demand for lower-skilled or unskilled workers as well. I think this needs to be acknowledged and dealt with too.”

title: Trump’s ‘Big Bill’ to cost students, universities billions
content:
Tweet
As warplanes roared overhead celebrating Independence Day on 4 July, United States President Donald J Trump signed into law a bill that dramatically downsizes the federal government’s role in financing America’s colleges and universities.
Dubbed (by Trump) the ‘One Big Beautiful Bill’ (OBBB, House of Representatives Bill), the budget reconciliation law alters how Pell Grants (available to the nation’s poorest students) are calculated in financial aid formulae.
It drastically reduces the amount of money students’ families can borrow for them under the federally insured student loan programme, imposes a graduate ‘earning test’ for programmes to maintain their access to federal student loans, and ends the Public Service Loan Forgiveness programme that former president Joe Biden had expanded four years ago.
The US$1 trillion cut to Medicare could result in 3.4 million college and university students losing their healthcare and the closure of rural hospitals run by universities.
The bill also increases the endowment tax for half of America’s colleges and universities.
Though the bill does not mention America’s historically black colleges and universities (HBCUs), because a disproportionate share of their students are economically disadvantaged, cuts to student aid, loans and Medicare will fall more heavily on students attending these institutions.
In total, the OBBB cuts more than a trillion dollars from the US budget over 10 years and increases the debt by US$4.2 trillion in order to pay for US$4.5 trillion in tax cuts – that will see the wealthiest 1% of American households save US$12,000 in taxes while the bill costs the poorest Americans US$1,600 a year.
Before signing the almost 900-page omnibus bill that was passed by the House of Representatives by two votes and in the Senate when Vice-President JD Vance broke a 50-50 tie, Trump called the OBBB: “The most popular bill ever signed in the history of our country.”
Three days before Trump signed the law, Secretary of Education Linda McMahon, whose department is now tasked with writing thousands of regulations required by the bill, took to X to thank Republican senators for passing the OBBB and said: “By establishing loan limits, the bill closes the spigot of federal subsidies that drive up college costs and burden families. The bill also simplifies and streamlines student loan repayment for millions of borrowers.”
Notwithstanding Trump’s comment about the OBBB’s popularity, critics of the bill, like Sameer Gadkaree , president and CEO of the Institute for College Access and Success (TICAS), who called it “one big mistake”, are more in line with public opinion.

Since all but one state is required to have a balanced budget, politicians will have two choices: the politically unpalatable option of raising taxes or finding the monies elsewhere, which often means cutting grants to public universities. “I suspect that every state is going to end up being in a position where the state itself has to simply raise taxes to make up the difference that the federal government revoked, because the states can't just simply say to all of the people in their state, the hundreds of thousands in Iowa [where Salisbury was when I interviewed him], for example, are going to lose their Medicaid. “So, the state is going to have to increase the amount of money it spends, which means they're going to have to increase taxes, right? And a whole bunch of states have started to talk about this already, like we’re going to have to increase taxes. We simply can't operate like we already want, right?” said Salisbury. According to Fansmith, in the past when faced with similar budgetary crises, states often turned to cutting their grants to the public universities and colleges because, since they charge tuition, they have what’s thought of as an independent revenue stream. Cuts to such major public institutions as the University of Michigan (UM) or the University of California (UCal) system are difficult enough for those institutions and students, though in some cases, UM and UCal, their endowments could help soften the blow. However, for the 50 publicly funded HBCUs, which educate 77% of the total number of HBCU students, state cuts are devastating because these institutions are chronically underfunded as it is. Ivy League endowment tax targets According to Nellums, the reworked endowment tax can be seen as another front in Trump’s battles with Harvard, Columbia, and other Ivy League universities. “We’ve done research that shows that a lot of the institutions that will primarily be impacted by the endowment taxes will be wealthier colleges and universities, such as Ivy League. It seems that the Trump administration is primarily targeting those institutions with the endowment tax.” Two months ago, speaking of their endowments (which in Harvard’s case is more than US$50 billion and in Columbia’s is almost US$15 billion), McMahon all but admitted as much. “It’s billions of dollars that could come into the government if this endowment revenue is taxed. I think the general public will look at that and say that might be a reasonable approach,” she said. The OBBB replaces the endowment tax of 1.4% brought in in 2017, during Trump’s first term, with three tiers; the calculations are based on dividing the endowment by the total student population. Institutions that have an endowment of between US$500,000 and US$750,000 per student will continue to pay 1.4%. Institutions that have an endowment of between US$750,000 and US$2 million will pay the rate of 4%. The rate for institutions with larger endowments is now 8%, a roughly six-fold increase. “For institutions falling into this category,” said Fansmith, “this is a massive increase in the tax they will be paying.” Yale University will now be paying more than US$280 million in taxes on its endowment of US$41billion, said its president, Maurie McInnis , who wrote to the Yale community that, “Taxing universities undermines the education and research that fuel life-saving medical breakthroughs, live-changing innovations, and the economic growth in communities across the country and around the globe.” According to Fansmith, the “net effect of these changes is that about half of institutions that were paying the endowment tax this year won’t have to pay going forward. But those institutions that are paying, in most cases, significantly more than they were paying before”. Increased government control of higher education At the end of our interview, Nellums turned from discussing the impact of the Trump administration’s cuts on critical cancer research, research into dementia, and how universities provide students with the opportunity to succeed and took aim at the Trump administration’s claim that universities are indoctrinating students with left-wing ideology and that they want to bring education back to the states. He told University World News: “What they’re doing is actually increasing the government’s role. They’re trying to have more of a foothold in higher education by also going after the accreditation process. “Make no mistake about it, this [the OBBB] is an attempt to cut funding, but [it is] also an effort to have a stronger hold on what these institutions are doing.”

title: Crisis looming for internationalisation industry in HE
content:
Tweet
University World News has published a variety of articles focusing on internationalisation in the context of recent dramatic geopolitical changes and their impact on higher education globally.
Hans de Wit analysed some of these discussions in his recent article, “What do we mean when we use the word ‘internationalisation’?” But one aspect of this important topic that these discussions have mostly ignored is the business angle of internationalisation.
While Altbach and De Wit wrote “When HE internationalisation operates as an industry” in University World News in April 2023, this trend has intensified in recent years, while at the same time the current geopolitical realities plus the advent and increasing sophistication of AI and related technologies require further analysis of its development and related challenges.
The internationalisation industry is not only big but also very diverse and serves a broad range of needs of the (higher) education sector in an era of increased marketisation and competition. It includes not-for-profit and for-profit entities, serving the public and-or the private good. Without question, internationalisation in its various aspects is now an industry, but, given these challenges, is it an industry in crisis?
Student mobility
The largest segment of the industry is student mobility – with almost seven million students globally mobile, according to UNESCO data for 2023 .
But there are many other, sometimes related, aspects as well. These include branch campuses – there are more than 300 worldwide, and their number is increasing – as well as other forms of transnational education (TNE), franchise operations, articulation programmes, binational universities, and others, mostly aimed at producing income for the partnering institutions.
Stephen Wilkins and Jeroen Huisman identify 11 forms of TNE. In addition, there are many international collaborative research enterprises of all kinds.
No one knows how extensive the internationalisation industry is, but our global estimate is that it is more than US$1.5 trillion annually. A few examples illustrate its size. Student mobility alone produces more than US$40 billion annually for the US economy, £37 billion (US$50 billion) for the United Kingdom, and AU$51 billion (or US$33 billion, where it is the country’s second largest export industry), to name the largest earners.
Countries also devote significant resources to internationalisation. For example, government-funded organisations such as Campus France, the German Academic Exchange Service (DAAD), the British Council, NUFFIC in the Netherlands, and EducationUSA and the Fulbright programme in the US are all engaged in the “soft power” of building international student and staff mobility and other programmes, for both political and economic objectives.
It is significant that NUFFIC, the British Council, and especially the Fulbright Program are now subject to severe budget cuts due to changing immigration policies, financial challenges, and populist influences.
These agencies and developments are just the tip of the iceberg of a massive industry that has been developed in the past half-century to serve the increasingly complex internationalisation nexus.
A largely invisible industry
It is not possible to fully describe and analyse this emerging industry. Not only is it too diverse and globally dispersed, but it is also highly opaque, with many players avoiding transparency concerning their activities. And the industry is undergoing significant change, especially in response to rapidly changing geopolitical realities and the increasing importance of artificial intelligence (AI).
The fact that a number of venture capital companies have invested in the industry in the past decade is a strong indication of its importance and potential from a financial perspective. For example, Times Higher Education, in addition to its publication and rankings, is now a data analytics company that builds on the data collected for its rankings as well as being a consultancy and sponsor of conferences and is owned by Inflexion Pvt Equity Partners LLP.
The scope and role of the industry are widespread and diverse and include a variety of consultancies that aid universities with their international programmes, companies that build residences for international students, companies that coordinate with banks to lend tuition funds to students going abroad, ranking companies that provide paid consultancies to help governments and institutions with improving their positions in the rankings and agents that recruit students for institutions that pay them.
Studyportals, as an example, is a Netherlands-based company that provides information on academic institutions and programmes worldwide to prospective students. It also works directly with academic institutions that pay for its services.
Another example of this industry is the recruitment agents. There are thousands of agents globally, with huge numbers in major sending countries, such as China and India.
The American International Recruitment Council, a membership organisation representing the agent community, has 400 institutional members globally and claims to provide ethical standards. The agent industry has come under much criticism for lack of transparency, ethical lapses, and falsifying admissions materials. But it is without doubt a key part of the student mobility ecosphere. Where is the industry heading? This is a period of considerable change, and quite likely crisis, for the internationalisation industry. Geopolitical tensions related to the rise of anti-immigrant and anti-intellectual sentiment combined with housing issues relating to international students in many of the main receiving countries, especially in the Anglosphere, may reshape mobility patterns and will likely reduce total numbers. Transnational education (TNE) operations may become more dominant as an alternative for student mobility, requiring big investments and risk assessments. This includes branch campuses of universities mostly in the Global North, joint degree programmes, franchising arrangements, and other initiatives to retain income and serve students while at the same time reducing international student numbers in the Global North. South-South cooperation and mobility will likely increase – both China and India have ambitious plans – although success is by no means assured. These changes create opportunities for consulting companies and firms involved in placing students in specific programmes. The advent of AI as a tool for selecting places to study and as a means for universities to communicate with prospective students from abroad is already in its early stages and may reshape or even upend the recruitment business. New partnership models may emerge to replace student mobility to fill skilled labour roles in high-income countries, such as tailor-made education schemes in middle- and low-income countries that prepare graduates for jobs abroad, as is already happening in the field of nursing in countries like the Philippines, Tunisia, and Albania. The internationalisation industry faces severe crises – it will no doubt survive so long as there is student mobility and international collaboration globally, and as long as there is a need for skilled labour from the developing world in the rich countries, but it has to adapt to new realities and quality and ethics concerns. Philip G Altbach (e-mail: altbach@bc.edu) and Hans de Wit (e-mail: dewitj@bc.edu) are both professor emeritus and distinguished fellow, Boston College Center for International Higher Education (CIHE), USA. title: Plan to withdraw living expenses for foreign PhD students
content:
Tweet
In a bid to boost the sagging number of Japanese doctoral students, the Japanese government is planning to reduce resources for international PhD students. The proposal aims to cut annual living allowances for foreigners, while Japanese students will continue to receive the funding.
The change proposed by a Ministry of Education expert panel made public on 26 June, which is expected to start from April 2026, is against a backdrop where 4,000 of the total 10,564 students in PhD programmes nationwide receiving JPY3 million (US$20,500) each in living expenses, were foreign students, according to the ministry.
Students from China comprised three-quarters of the 39% of PhD students that are international students. Lawmakers claim that many international students fund their living expenses privately.
However, experts have pointed out that weakening aid to foreign students could gravely impact Japanese government plans to attract foreign students and top international professionals to contribute to national employment and research programmes. For example, Japan faces a shortage of almost 750,000 IT engineers by 2040.
Futao Huang, a professor at the Research Institute for Higher Education, Hiroshima University, said the proposal “appears contradictory to Japan’s broader goal of attracting and retaining highly skilled international talent”.
“Cutting living allowances for international doctoral students could discourage talented individuals from choosing Japan, especially when other countries are increasing support to build global research capacity,” Huang said.
Retaining high-performing international graduates could help address skill shortages and strengthen Japan’s position in the global knowledge economy, he added via email.
The proposed change addresses SPRING (Support Pioneering Research Initiated by the Next Generation), implemented in 2021 by the Japan Science and Technology Agency to increase assistance to Japanese students.
It aimed to tackle the domestic decline in PhD enrolment – 2024 domestic PhD enrolment declined 12% compared to a decade ago, while foreigners rose by 35% in the same period, according to official data, which also points out that Japanese students cited financial difficulties and concerns over employment prospects as reasons for not enrolling in PhD programmes.
Political backdrop
Experts also point to the political backdrop behind the proposals. Japanese media reported the SPRING programme came under fire from the ruling conservative Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) in March when it was discussed as part of “excessive reliance on international students and an economic security risk.”
LDP lawmaker Haruko Arimura, referring to limiting foreign students, was quoted in the daily Japan News on March 26 as saying: “without clearly establishing the principle of supporting Japanese students, we cannot gain public understanding”.
“Accepting foreign nationals as immigrants is becoming a major domestic political campaign issue,” pointed out adjunct researcher Kazuyuki Suwa, who teaches Chinese language at Daito Bunka University.
Suwa views the proposal as a blow to Japan’s international profile, referring to Japanese universities as an opportunity to attract foreign students, given the current lower exchange rate for the Japanese currency, the yen, and university tuition fees at JPY 1.2 million annually, considered reasonable by international standards.
Mitsunobu Kano, a professor in the faculty of interdisciplinary science at Okayama University and an expert on the panel advising the ministry on the proposed reforms, explained the change supports the core aim of the SPRING programme – to increase the number of Japanese researchers by providing assistance.
“The programme supports applications from Japanese students, which is the original intention of the Japanese government. There is a critical need to raise the research profile of universities, and aspiring Japanese doctoral students need assistance,” he told University World News.
Kano does not expect a decline in foreign doctoral students in Japan. He noted that top-level students, including foreigners, will continue to receive SPRING research funding as stipulated in the SPRING goals. Financial aid for research – around JPY 400,000 per year – would continue to be available regardless of nationality.
Concern over increase in Chinese students
The increase in the number of Chinese researchers in Japanese universities is also leading to new screening guidelines for foreign doctoral students that became effective in 2022.
While no issues have been made public by officials, policymakers refer to the need to protect against intellectual property theft and cyberattacks, which they see as posing a national threat.
On average, international students are less than 5% of those in tertiary education compared to 20% in the United Kingdom. Japan has set a goal of increasing the low figure to 30% by 2033. The government’s 2023 MIRAI (Mutual Understanding, Intellectual Relations, and Academic Exchange Initiative) Programme – a short-term youth exchange scheme to invite undergraduate and graduate students to Japan – set a goal of achieving 400,000 foreign students by 2033, including increasing international doctorate students to 33% from the current 21%. The policy also aims to increase foreign graduate employment to 60% from the current 48% that includes vocational students.
