title: Bremen University cancels renowned Jewish researcher
content:
Tweet
The University of Bremen has cancelled an event featuring psychoanalyst Iris Hefets on its premises.
The university argued that the organisation Hefets belongs to, Jewish Voice for Just Peace in the Middle East, has been classified as “reliably assessed as extremist” by the Verfassungsschutz, Germany’s Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution.
Hefets is an internationally renowned specialist on trauma research and Holocaust remembrance and was to give a presentation on ‘Schweigen und Schuld – Psychologische Mechanismen im Umgang mit dem Genozid in Gaza’ (Silence and Guilt – Psychological Mechanisms in Dealing with the Genocide in Gaza).
Organisers of the event included Bremen University’s student union.
In response to university rector Jutta Günther announcing the cancellation, an alternative venue was provided by Bremen’s Evangelical Zionskirche church.
Hefets is a board member of the association Jewish Voice for Just Peace in the Middle East – EJJP Deutschland, which was founded in Berlin in 2003 as the German section of the umbrella organisation European Jews for a Just Peace, launched one year earlier in Amsterdam, Netherlands.
The organisation’s mission is to join with Jews in Europe and globally in “asserting that the Israeli colonisation and occupation of Palestine is not carried out in the name and in the interest of Jews worldwide”.
The Verfassungsschutz (VS) bases its classification of Jewish Voice as “pro-Palestinian and extremist” on the latter’s support of the Boycott, Divestment, and Sanctions (BDS) movement and its critique of Israel, which is viewed as hostile to Israel and antisemitic as defined by the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA).
The annual VS report issued by Germany’s Ministry of the Interior refers to “Jüdische Stimme” in the context of “left-wing extremism” and “extremism relating to foreign countries” with regard to its participation in pro-Palestinian demonstrations following the Hamas attack on Israel on 7 October 2023.
In a letter to the Bremen University student union, Rector Günther, with reference to the 2024 VS report, points to a “concrete danger” of the contents of the event clashing with Germany’s free democratic liberal order as stipulated in the Federal Constitution.
She argued that an event featuring a board member of Jewish Voice, an organisation classified by the report as “reliably assessed as extremist”, as a lecturer therefore cannot be permitted.
The University of Bremen stressed that it is responsible for all its members, in this context in particular its Jewish members. In a letter to Günther, Sabine Broeck, retired professor of American Studies, Gender Studies, and Transatlantic Black Diaspora Studies at the University of Bremen, sharply criticised her former institution’s decision not to permit Hefets’ lecture, also pointing out that Hefets was awarded the Göttingen Friedenspreis (peace prize) in 2019 for her activities in Jewish Voice. Broeck argued that the VS classification of Jewish Voice “brings this government body in line with a series of fascist precedent cases, the return of which the University of Bremen in particular has been warning of publicly for some weeks”. “This classification restricts public debate and critique – which is also extremely damaging to academic freedom at our university,” she said. Broeck maintained that the rector’s decision constitutes “anticipatory loyalty towards a government body which denies a Jewish intellectual and the organisation she campaigns for public space for discussion and criminalises her activities”. She said that this is “not only morally disgusting for a German university management in times of growing fascism; it is also directly antisemitic”. Broeck claimed that “overzealous self-styled anti-antisemitism on the part of German state authorities and institutions is in itself in turn resulting in antisemitic action”. Between 7 October 2023 and 31 January 2024, the European Legal Support Center (ELSC) documented 202 cases of political repression, including 68 threats of legal action, such as administrative civil rights complaints, as well as 57 cases of harassment, intimidation, or violence against individuals or groups expressing solidarity with the Palestinian people. The Index of Repression the ELSC published in collaboration with the University of London-based research agency Forensic Architecture last May lists a total of 766 cases since 2019 in which German government institutions have taken action against individuals or organisations demonstrating solidarity with Palestine. Included are restrictions of academic freedom, police measures, and cancellation of events. In this context, the share of Jewish individuals involved is disproportionately high in comparison to the overall share of Jews among the German population. According to the Jewish organisation Diaspora Alliance, around a quarter of the 84 respective cases recorded in 2023 concerned Jewish individuals or groups. Hefets commented on the University of Bremen’s action that Germany, having based its own identity on Jews being “ideal” and equating Jewishness with the State of Israel, cannot tolerate Jewish dissent as expressed, for instance, by Jewish Voice. This would otherwise threaten German “identity” and have a “destabilising effect” on what German politicians refer to as the Staatsräson, that is, the political identity of the state. title: Why nearly two-thirds of Africa’s students experience stress
content:
Tweet
Nearly two-thirds of university students in Africa experience stress, with Sudanese students the most severely affected, according to a study that also focuses on some of the measures that higher education institutions can adopt to support students’ mental health and academic performance.
The study , titled ‘Burden of perceived stress among university students in Africa: A systematic review and meta-analysis’, published in BMC Public Health this July demonstrates “the overall combined magnitude of perceived stress and its predictors among university students”.
It was authored by Setegn Fentahun, Gidey Rtbey, Girum Nakie, Fantahun Andualem, Techilo Tinsae, Getasew Kibralew, Getachew Tesfaw, Tigist Kifle, Mulualem Kelebie and Gebresilassie Tadesse from the Institute of Public Health based at the College of Medicine and Health Sciences at the University of Gondar, Ethiopia.
The study said that there “is a dearth of representative pooled data” regarding the prevalence of perceived stress among African university students, which is why the research could be “crucial” for mental health professionals, educators, and policymakers to establish focused interventions aimed at lowering stress and enhancing students’ academic performance and general well-being.
Students’ stress levels
Using a total of 26 primary articles, based on studies conducted in eight African countries, the systematic review and meta-analysis, which used several databases, showed that the overall combined prevalence of perceived stress among the 7,828 university students included in the study was 64.72%.This was comparable with previous studies conducted in Thailand, the Middle East and North Africa.
According to the study, the similarity in the findings across regions can be explained because academic pressure, performance-related concerns, workload, and worries regarding future job opportunities, are common primary sources of students’ perceived stress.
“However, African higher education students frequently encounter additional structural difficulties that could contribute to increased stress, including frequent political instability that affects the educational system, overcrowded classrooms, financial difficulties, and inadequate counselling services,” the study explained.
Furthermore, the study said, a possible reason for the observed higher prevalence of perceived stress in university students in general might be related to the nature of higher education.
In this context, students are being faced with a variety of shifting circumstances, such as adjusting to an unfamiliar environment away from home, the cost of education and financial strain because of a lack of income, shifts in social networks including new relationships, handling autonomy for the first time, and being forced to manage the academic obligations of university.
Why different countries’ students experience HE differently
The study found that the highest overall pooled prevalence of perceived stress was observed in Sudanese university students, followed by Tunisia and Uganda, and the lowest combined perceived stress was detected in Ethiopian university students, followed by Nigeria and Egypt.
Sudanese university students have encountered persistent economic and political instability, disturbances in the higher education system, financial constraints, and inadequate availability of mental health services.
In March 2025, University World News also reported on a study which indicated that university students in the war-torn regions of Sudan experience high levels of stress, anxiety and depression due to the ongoing armed conflict since mid-April 2023.
According to the study, differences in the perceived stress levels of students across the continent could be attributed to variations in sample size, socio-economic differences, and cultural variation in African countries.
Differences in teaching strategies, grading systems and curriculums, as well as disparities in the availability of resources among African universities, may also be a reason for differences across the continent as students may feel more stressed when they have inadequate access to counselling services, academic support, or sufficient infrastructure, according to the study. Reasons for students’ perceived stress In addition to the changing circumstances of students, which contribute to perceived stress levels, lifestyle factors also emerged as challenges. The study added that university students also frequently have poor eating habits, little exercise, and irregular sleep schedules. Problems with sleep were highlighted by the researchers. Notably, stress levels increased by 2.29 times for participants who struggled to sleep. University students who experience sleep problems may become even more stressed since inadequate sleep can result in a prolonged disrupted sleep cycle, which affects learning, mental health and cognitive function, according to the study. The meta-analysis also showed that students with financial problems were 1.58 times more likely to experience perceived stress, which can impair academic achievement, and have a detrimental impact on a student’s emotional and physical health. What can be done? Based on the findings, the study put forward several measures to deal with the stress levels students in Africa appear to be dealing with. The researchers called upon universities, stakeholders, and policymakers in the higher education context in Africa to work collaboratively to establish conditions that promote students’ academic achievement and general well-being. “It is also crucial that universities provide focused stress-reduction programmes such as online counselling services, which would give students easily available support – particularly for those who have busy schedules and are embarrassed to ask for help in person – and develop peer support groups in which students can exchange stress-related experiences and coping mechanisms,” the study said. “Moreover, working on the underlying causes of stress and handling fundamental problems, including enhancing educational resources, expanding student financial assistance programmes and emergency funds, providing awareness campaigns on sleep hygiene, and establishing encouraging educational settings, are essential to reduce the burdens of perceived stress among university students in Africa,” the researchers said.

title: NVIDIA’s AI university part of new industry-academia drive
content:
Tweet
Plans are underway to set up an AI university in India in collaboration with California-based technology company NVIDIA, a major global supplier of artificial intelligence hardware and software, according to an announcement by the state government of Andhra Pradesh (AP) in Southern India.
But the move also reflects a growing trend in India for universities to partner with industry to skill more industry-ready graduates for the country’s burgeoning IT and AI sector.
Many global companies are setting up in India, in part driven by global moves away from China, as well as being driven to diversify locations by the United States administration’s tariff policies, while Indian tech companies are growing, creating huge demand for tech talent.
The initiative with NVIDIA, announced in June, will build on current collaboration with NVIDIA in the southern state. Nara Chandrababu Naidu, chief minister of Andhra Pradesh, recently announced that with support from NVIDIA for curriculum and training, 10,000 engineering students will receive skill training in the next two years.
Naidu said in a post on X on 7 June: “Andhra Pradesh is welcoming bold initiatives to lead India’s AI revolution. Under the leadership of (AP) Minister for IT Nara Lokesh, we have entered into an MoU with NVIDIA to build a strong and inclusive AI ecosystem in the state.
“As many as 500 AI startups from AP will gain access to its Inception Programme for global exposure and key resources.”
He was referring to NVIDIA’s Inception, a free programme designed to nurture startups, providing access to cutting-edge technology, marketing support, and opportunities to connect with NVIDIA experts.
“Further, plans are underway to establish India’s first AI university in collaboration with NVIDIA for shaping the infrastructure and research capabilities. From education and skilling to research and innovation, this initiative is laying the foundation for a Swarna Andhra Pradesh,” he said, referring to the ‘Golden’ AP.
Experts noted that state governments like Andhra Pradesh were keen to turn academic institutions into ‘industry-ready’ talent hubs.
Shift in university teaching
“India’s higher education landscape is rapidly transforming to meet evolving economic and technological demands.
“Academic institutions are shifting from traditional, theory-based learning to a focus on industry-aligned skills, real-world experience, and entrepreneurial mindsets,” said a just-released report from Nasscom (National Association of Software and Service Companies), the trade body representing India’s US$283 billion tech industry, focused on making the country a global hub for IT services and innovation.
Nasscom emphasised in the report released last week titled “Building the Next Generation of Tech Professionals: Transformative Trends Reshaping Academia” that global and Indian IT companies are “embedding hands-on industry-aligned learning into academic pathways”.
“In embracing these shifts, academia is no longer positioned merely as a responder to industry demand but rather as a proactive partner in the co-creation of talent,” Achyuta Ghosh, senior director and head of Nasscom Insights, said in the report.
The report said institutions are partnering with industry to offer specialised training in line with skills sought by industry. The report pointed out that “78% of recruiters in India now prioritise skills over formal qualifications”, with Indian centres of multinational corporations, and IT firms leading the transition at 85% and 71%, respectively.” Three-quarters of over 200 engineering-focused Indian academic institutions surveyed by Nasscom said they were collaborating with industry partners to help bridge the skills gap. Collaboration includes “assisting in curriculum redesign through insights into current industry practices and needs, supporting faculty development, organising hackathons and workshops, engaging in collaborative research, facilitating internships and live project opportunities.” For example, Bangalore-based Indian tech giant Infosys is collaborating with Sandip University, a private university in Maharashtra state, to upskill educators through faculty development programmes and provide special courses and certifications for students on new technologies such as AI, machine learning, and blockchain technology using its free-access Springboard digital learning platform. The report noted: “These partnerships are no longer confined to individual colleges or universities; they are increasingly expanding to the state level, with state education authorities joining hands with industry to enhance student upskilling efforts.” Growth in Industry collaboration Rangan Banerjee, director of the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Delhi, told University World News: “We are seeing a very significant growth in industry collaborations. We are also seeing very high growth rates in terms of funding.” However, he noted that in the Indian ecosystem, “government and public funding is significantly higher than industry funding.” “We started with a smaller base from industry, but we are also getting a lot of global industry, and we are looking at a whole host of different models, including industry-government-academia, sometimes known as the triple helix model.” He noted that IIT Delhi already has some links and collaborations with NVIDIA. He pointed to more government-industry-university research models for IITs in future. “Industry is increasingly relying on technology development and research – there is a very clear trend in that. The ecosystem still has a long way to go, but it is growing.” Banerjee pointed to the timing of the AP announcement as interesting. “This is something more in terms of the Andhra Pradesh government and the CM wanting to push in certain domains and establish that Andhra Pradesh can be a hub in high-end areas, and they may have had some conversations with NVIDIA and others,” he said. “The talent chain, tariffs, and national perspectives have been the key drivers,” he added, referring to recent US trade and technology policies, which are upending traditional talent chains and technology routes, mainly between the US and China. Earlier this month India’s Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, approved a Research Development and Innovation (RDI) Scheme with funding of approximately US$12 billion. “Aimed at enhancing private sector participation in cutting-edge research,” according to the official statement, the funds will be disbursed by India’s newly established overarching science funding agency, the Anusandhan National Research Foundation (ANRF). This may lead to more collaborative funding with universities and institutions like the IITs, according to experts. Foreign universities interested in Industry Foreign universities planning to set up in India are also showing an interest in industry tie ups, in particular to enhance the employability of their graduates within India. Five foreign branch campuses have been approved to operate in India so far, with another 15 or so slated for this year . “You’ll start to see foreign universities announce strategic partnerships with Indian industry,” predicted Adrian Mutton, CEO of Acumen, an education consultancy advising universities globally that want to set up in Asia. “Within 12 to 18 months there will be several other large corporations announcing the same thing. I think you're going to see this more and more,” he told University World News. “A lot of the work that we’ve been doing lately is with those foreign universities [that] are looking at going into India and essentially getting their curriculum fit for industry…. So that has already started.” “The advantage that NVIDIA has is it will have more money to pay faculty as a private sector company,” Mutton said. “You’re already seeing IIT Bombay and other notable institutions across India now accepting private sector individuals to come in and have teaching positions in their universities.” NVIDIA in Taiwan For several years NVIDIA has been collaborating with universities in Taiwan, where NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang was born, and it has become a testbed for university collaboration with NVIDIA. Last year the company donated around US$1.54 million towards an AI research centre project along with other collaborative projects at National Taiwan University (NTU). NTU President Wen-Chang Chen said at the time the university partnered with NVIDIA to establish the AI University Centre to integrate AI into teaching, research, and entrepreneurship. The initiative will train AI instructors to incorporate AI into curricula across all departments and foster research in various AI fields. Additionally, it will encourage faculty and students to leverage AI technology for entrepreneurial ventures, supported by external resources. Other universities in Taiwan have smaller collaboration projects with NVIDIA. Several universities in Taiwan last year reported a spike in enrolment enquiries after they were listed by Huang in a speech at NTU last year as collaborating with the tech giant.

title: Student choice HE system fails to deliver enough engineers
content:
Tweet
The lack of engineering graduates coming out of United Kingdom universities has highlighted the failure of the demand-led student choice system of higher education to produce the skilled workforce essential to driving economic renewal, which is the Labour government’s top priority, claims an industry leader.
However, that’s not all working against universities enrolling more students on engineering and technology courses – with the high cost of expanding places and the requirement of A-levels in mathematics and physics for entry to many first degrees restricting access, particularly for women and less advantaged applicants.
With the United Kingdom facing mounting challenges – from delays to infrastructure and renewable energy projects to enabling AI-driven industries to thrive – the head of a not-for-profit organisation working to inspire the next generation of engineers has warned of a mismatch between the small number of UK undergraduates studying engineering and technology and growing job vacancies in key industries, including green energy.
Hilary Leevers, chief executive of EngineeringUK , said that on their estimate there were only 6.1% of UK undergraduates in 2020-21 enrolled in engineering and technology first degrees, while these sectors accounted for 25% of job adverts and 19% of the UK workforce.
Too much to chance
Leevers said that while the demand-driven higher education system may be “nice in principle”, it “leaves too much to chance”.
In a new book, she urges universities – and the government – to intervene, saying: “Essential workforce needs can’t be left entirely to student choice.”
Her chapter, “Shaping Higher Education: Driving Economic Prosperity and Sustainability Through Engineering and Technology” is part of a collection of articles in a new book, Making Equal – New Visions for Opportunity and Growth (Emerald Publishing), edited by Graeme Atherton and Peter John, to mark the 125th anniversary of Ruskin College, Oxford, which was founded in 1899 with trade union support to offer working-class adults career-focused higher education.
Leevers says many UK companies are struggling to fill vacancies, and the skills shortage threatens economic prosperity and the nation’s capacity to address environmental and technological challenges. It is also driving up salaries in engineering, which are 30% higher than the national average.
She claims that the UK further education system is more responsive to labour market needs than universities, despite over 40% of engineering-related jobs requiring a degree.
Lack of women
The lack of women enrolling in engineering and technology undergraduate degrees is a major problem, standing at just 18.5%, according to the Institute of Engineering and Technology.
Representation is higher on engineering and technology postgraduate courses, at around 26-28% for women.
However, the lack of diversity goes wider, with disabled students making up just 10.5% of those in engineering and tech first degrees and those coming from areas with low higher education participation rates representing 11.2% of students compared with 32.4% coming from the highest participation areas.
“Interestingly, engineering and technology degrees had a higher proportion of UK minority ethnic entrants than other subjects, particularly Asian students,” said Leevers.
Physics
She said widening participation is challenged by many engineering courses requiring mathematics and physics at A-levels for entry, especially as 400 secondary schools lack even one qualified physics teacher. Some institutions, such as the New Model Institute for Technology and Engineering (NMITE) in Hereford and The Engineering and Design Initiative in London (TEDI-London), have taken a more innovative approach to recruitment, weighting students’ motivation and potential to succeed rather than focusing on entry criteria. Leevers urges others to follow and to use foundation years, summer schools, and targeted support to help level the playing field further and unlock hidden talent. Such initiatives are welcomed by engineering education leaders, with Johnny Rich, Chief Executive of the Engineering Professors’ Council, telling University World News that nearly half of all engineering courses now no longer require physics A level (or equivalent). “That’s a wise approach given the shortages of physics teachers and that many engineering academics feel the A-level physics curriculum doesn’t map across to what students would need to know anyway,” he said. Disconnect between students and labour market Rich told University World News he agreed with Leevers about the disconnect between student ambitions and the labour market, saying: “Student choice dominates the availability of courses, but there’s nothing to ensure that matches the talent pipeline that employers need. “It’s particularly problematic in engineering, which is further complicated by the fact that universities cannot afford to expand their engineering courses to meet the rise, in recent years, of applications, because the funding falls so far below the actual cost of providing high-quality courses. “Whenever there is a squeeze on places, it impacts access for underrepresented groups. “Given engineering’s historic record as a key driver of social mobility, that means a triple whammy for the government’s missions on growth, opportunity, and regional development.” Professor Beverley Gibbs, director of the Dyson Institute of Engineering and Technology , a private higher education institution specialising in engineering and innovation based in Wiltshire, told University World News that the lack of women studying engineering hasn’t budged in the 40 years since she was an engineering apprentice in 1986. Her class back then had just 14% women in it. She said the 6.1% of undergraduates studying engineering sounded about right but increased to 12.4% if computer science was included. Participation varies by sub-discipline “The participation rates for women vary widely by sub-discipline, with electrical and mechanical engineering being lower and biomedical engineering much higher. “This appears to be a very Western problem, as international comparisons have shown,” she stated. Gibbs urged caution on the lack of women studying physics and math at A-level, saying: “Medicine also requires those subjects at A-level, and medical schools are full of women.” She believes women may be more attracted when the people’s side of engineering is visible. “If true, this is a failing of us as a profession, and I’ve argued in the past that engineering is all about people, not things,” she said. The Dyson Institute is a member of GuildHE, a group of 70 universities, university colleges, and specialist institutions focused on delivering vocational and technical higher education. Better guidance Another member of the group is Ravensbourne University, based in London’s North Greenwich digital hub, where Professor of Digital Media Simon Robertshaw, told University World News that young people considering joining the six million-strong engineering and tech workforce need better guidance about the opportunities available to flourish. “Especially women and those from lower-income backgrounds and ethnic minority groups, they need role models in the fields and impartial advice on how to get in. “We try to break down the barriers by co-creating our digital curricula with industry and embed real-world projects and placements,” he said. Underrepresented Stephanie Baxter, head of policy at the Institution of Engineering and Technology (IET), told University World News that despite women remaining significantly under-represented in engineering and technology, both in university enrolments and across the workforce, some STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) disciplines are seeing encouraging levels of female participation, with biological and sport sciences (50.8%), subjects allied to medicine (79%), and medicine and dentistry (64%). “However, the imbalance persists beyond education. Women make up only 26.7% of the STEM workforce, despite representing 47.5% of the overall working population. And as seniority increases, female representation declines even further,’ she noted. Baxter said that their latest skills survey highlights a concerning trend: only 54% of engineering employers in England, 47% in Wales, and 44% in Scotland believe the current education system is fit for purpose. “To close the skills gap and unlock the full potential of our future workforce, we must reimagine how we present and support disciplines like engineering. “By doing so, we can inspire broader participation, raise aspirations, and equip students with the creativity and problem-solving skills that are vital to our economy. “Improving gender parity – and diversity more broadly – isn’t just good for business. It’s essential for innovation, collaboration, and the long-term health of our society and economy,” she concluded. Nic Mitchell is a UK-based freelance journalist and PR consultant specialising in European and international higher education. He blogs at www.delacourcommunications.com .

With the United Kingdom facing mounting challenges – from delays to infrastructure and renewable energy projects to enabling AI-driven industries to thrive – the head of a not-for-profit organisation working to inspire the next generation of engineers has warned of a mismatch between the small number of UK undergraduates studying engineering and technology and growing job vacancies in key industries, including green energy.
Hilary Leevers, chief executive of EngineeringUK , said that on their estimate there were only 6.1% of UK undergraduates in 2020-21 enrolled in engineering and technology first degrees, while these sectors accounted for 25% of job adverts and 19% of the UK workforce.
Too much to chance
Leevers said that while the demand-driven higher education system may be “nice in principle”, it “leaves too much to chance”.
In a new book, she urges universities – and the government – to intervene, saying: “Essential workforce needs can’t be left entirely to student choice.”
Her chapter, “Shaping Higher Education: Driving Economic Prosperity and Sustainability Through Engineering and Technology” is part of a collection of articles in a new book, Making Equal – New Visions for Opportunity and Growth (Emerald Publishing), edited by Graeme Atherton and Peter John, to mark the 125th anniversary of Ruskin College, Oxford, which was founded in 1899 with trade union support to offer working-class adults career-focused higher education.
Leevers says many UK companies are struggling to fill vacancies, and the skills shortage threatens economic prosperity and the nation’s capacity to address environmental and technological challenges. It is also driving up salaries in engineering, which are 30% higher than the national average.
She claims that the UK further education system is more responsive to labour market needs than universities, despite over 40% of engineering-related jobs requiring a degree.
Lack of women
The lack of women enrolling in engineering and technology undergraduate degrees is a major problem, standing at just 18.5%, according to the Institute of Engineering and Technology.
Representation is higher on engineering and technology postgraduate courses, at around 26-28% for women.
However, the lack of diversity goes wider, with disabled students making up just 10.5% of those in engineering and tech first degrees and those coming from areas with low higher education participation rates representing 11.2% of students compared with 32.4% coming from the highest participation areas.
“Interestingly, engineering and technology degrees had a higher proportion of UK minority ethnic entrants than other subjects, particularly Asian students,” said Leevers.
Physics
She said widening participation is challenged by many engineering courses requiring mathematics and physics at A-levels for entry, especially as 400 secondary schools lack even one qualified physics teacher. Some institutions, such as the New Model Institute for Technology and Engineering (NMITE) in Hereford and The Engineering and Design Initiative in London (TEDI-London), have taken a more innovative approach to recruitment, weighting students’ motivation and potential to succeed rather than focusing on entry criteria. Leevers urges others to follow and to use foundation years, summer schools, and targeted support to help level the playing field further and unlock hidden talent. Such initiatives are welcomed by engineering education leaders, with Johnny Rich, Chief Executive of the Engineering Professors’ Council, telling University World News that nearly half of all engineering courses now no longer require physics A level (or equivalent). “That’s a wise approach given the shortages of physics teachers and that many engineering academics feel the A-level physics curriculum doesn’t map across to what students would need to know anyway,” he said. Disconnect between students and labour market Rich told University World News he agreed with Leevers about the disconnect between student ambitions and the labour market, saying: “Student choice dominates the availability of courses, but there’s nothing to ensure that matches the talent pipeline that employers need. “It’s particularly problematic in engineering, which is further complicated by the fact that universities cannot afford to expand their engineering courses to meet the rise, in recent years, of applications, because the funding falls so far below the actual cost of providing high-quality courses. “Whenever there is a squeeze on places, it impacts access for underrepresented groups. “Given engineering’s historic record as a key driver of social mobility, that means a triple whammy for the government’s missions on growth, opportunity, and regional development.” Professor Beverley Gibbs, director of the Dyson Institute of Engineering and Technology , a private higher education institution specialising in engineering and innovation based in Wiltshire, told University World News that the lack of women studying engineering hasn’t budged in the 40 years since she was an engineering apprentice in 1986. Her class back then had just 14% women in it. She said the 6.1% of undergraduates studying engineering sounded about right but increased to 12.4% if computer science was included. Participation varies by sub-discipline “The participation rates for women vary widely by sub-discipline, with electrical and mechanical engineering being lower and biomedical engineering much higher. “This appears to be a very Western problem, as international comparisons have shown,” she stated. Gibbs urged caution on the lack of women studying physics and math at A-level, saying: “Medicine also requires those subjects at A-level, and medical schools are full of women.” She believes women may be more attracted when the people’s side of engineering is visible. “If true, this is a failing of us as a profession, and I’ve argued in the past that engineering is all about people, not things,” she said. The Dyson Institute is a member of GuildHE, a group of 70 universities, university colleges, and specialist institutions focused on delivering vocational and technical higher education. Better guidance Another member of the group is Ravensbourne University, based in London’s North Greenwich digital hub, where Professor of Digital Media Simon Robertshaw, told University World News that young people considering joining the six million-strong engineering and tech workforce need better guidance about the opportunities available to flourish. “Especially women and those from lower-income backgrounds and ethnic minority groups, they need role models in the fields and impartial advice on how to get in. “We try to break down the barriers by co-creating our digital curricula with industry and embed real-world projects and placements,” he said. Underrepresented Stephanie Baxter, head of policy at the Institution of Engineering and Technology (IET), told University World News that despite women remaining significantly under-represented in engineering and technology, both in university enrolments and across the workforce, some STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) disciplines are seeing encouraging levels of female participation, with biological and sport sciences (50.8%), subjects allied to medicine (79%), and medicine and dentistry (64%). “However, the imbalance persists beyond education. Women make up only 26.7% of the STEM workforce, despite representing 47.5% of the overall working population. And as seniority increases, female representation declines even further,’ she noted. Baxter said that their latest skills survey highlights a concerning trend: only 54% of engineering employers in England, 47% in Wales, and 44% in Scotland believe the current education system is fit for purpose. “To close the skills gap and unlock the full potential of our future workforce, we must reimagine how we present and support disciplines like engineering. “By doing so, we can inspire broader participation, raise aspirations, and equip students with the creativity and problem-solving skills that are vital to our economy. “Improving gender parity – and diversity more broadly – isn’t just good for business. It’s essential for innovation, collaboration, and the long-term health of our society and economy,” she concluded. Nic Mitchell is a UK-based freelance journalist and PR consultant specialising in European and international higher education. He blogs at www.delacourcommunications.com .

title: Growth in private HE opens access but raises concerns
Three more international campuses set to open in Dubai
content:
Tweet
Three more international universities are set to open campuses in Dubai during the 2025 to 2026 academic year.
The universities will boost the 37 international branch campuses that already exist, which expand access to higher education but arguably have negligible impact on research and innovation, the core drivers of the knowledge-based economy.
This necessitates a shift toward enhancing investment in research capacity, academic-industry linkages, and evidence-driven policymaking, among others.
In a press release on 2 July, the Knowledge and Human Development Authority (KHDA) announced that the universities confirmed to commence operations include the Indian Institute of Management Ahmedabad (IIM Ahmedabad), the American University of Beirut, and Saudi Arabia’s Fakeeh College for Medical Sciences. Additionally, the KHDA noted that discussions are ongoing with several other international universities.
Dr Wafi Dawood, CEO of the Strategic Development Sector at KHDA said: “This initiative aligns with the social and economic goals of the Dubai Economic Agenda D33 and the Education 33 Strategy , which represents a transformative vision for Dubai’s education system”.
The goal of the Education 33 Strategy’s global university attraction project is to establish a cutting-edge educational environment that combines national and transnational programmes that fund education, scientific research, and cross-border cooperation in a range of economic sectors.
According to KHDA, by 2033, 50% of students in the emirate’s higher education institutions will be foreigners, adding AED 5.6 billion (US$1.52 billion) to the gross domestic product (GDP) and placing Dubai among the top 10 locations in the world for university study.
“Our aim is to enhance the global competitiveness of Dubai’s graduates, increase educational tourism tenfold by 2033, integrate a new generation of Emiratis into the workforce and future sectors, and contribute to doubling Dubai’s economy over the next decade, positioning the city among the world’s top three economic hubs,” Dawood noted.
The UAE is currently ranked second among the top five hosting countries for foreign international campuses, after China and followed by Singapore, Malaysia, and Qatar, according to the March 2023 Branch Campus Listing prepared by the University of Miami’s Cross-Border Education Research Team (C-BERT).
Toward a more ‘multipolar TNE’
Dr Tim Rottleb at Brandenburg University of Technology Cottbus-Senftenberg in Germany, told University World News: “The opening of three new foreign campuses in Dubai highlights the city’s growing role as an emerging hub in the global landscape of transnational higher education (TNE).”
Rottleb, who is the author of the 2024 study “Offshore campus development and the worlding of Dubai as an international education hub”, noted that this indicates that traditional Western networks are losing their dominance over the international education market, which is becoming more diverse.
“The fact that these new campuses include institutions from outside the usual Anglo-American sphere shows how places like Dubai are actively cultivating new academic and economic ties,” he added.
He said this development suggests a shift toward a more multipolar TNE system, where new centres can emerge. “At the same time, it underscores the strategic ambitions of Dubai to position itself as a key node in these evolving global networks,” Rottleb pointed out.
Expanding access to HE
Professor Lokman Meho, based at the American University of Beirut in Lebanon, sees the addition of three new foreign campuses as a reflection of a strategic move by Dubai to expand access to higher education for nationals and, more importantly, key expatriate and neighbouring communities – Lebanese, Indian, and Saudi – within the United Arab Emirates (UAE).
While Dubai is currently ranked 72nd in the QS Best Student Cities 2025 rankings, it is, according to Meho, becoming a major host of international students through wisely investing in higher education institutions aligned with its D33 and E33 agendas to promote knowledge-based economic development.
“As a fast-growing, cosmopolitan city with a deep need for quality higher education, Dubai is moving fast on its ambition to be a Top 10 Student City,” Meho told University World News.
“These campuses will serve families who prefer to keep their children nearby, reduce the financial and logistical burdens of studying abroad, and respond to rising safety and visa concerns in traditional host countries,” he added. Andy Pacino , Director of Studies at EF Education First, has no doubt that the increase in the number of foreign campuses in Dubai contributes positively to the region’s HE landscape. According to Pacino, institutions like the University of Manchester and the University of Birmingham bring global expertise and advanced research capabilities to the region. “What they also offer is international collaboration that can foster and encourage innovation and human capital development,” he told University World News. Local vs satellite campuses However, Pacino highlighted the current rankings gap between local institutions and their foreign satellite campuses. “Not many branch campuses figure in either regional or international rankings, and local institutions are favoured rather than the satellite campuses. That could be put down to recent challenges in research output, integration with the local community, and visibility (or lack of it) of branch campus contributions,” Pacino explained. The home campuses of several foreign HE institutions with a presence in Dubai are ranked among the top 200 globally in the QS World University Rankings for 2026. These include the University of Manchester Dubai (35th), the University of Birmingham Dubai (76th), Curtin University Dubai (183rd), and the University of Wollongong Dubai (184th). In contrast, the 2024 local ranking for universities in the UAE identified only 4 foreign branch campuses, and the regional and international rankings have not included any foreign branch campuses. As University World News reported the list of 34 top research universities includes only four foreign branch campuses, namely New York University Abu Dhabi (group 1, outstanding), the University of Wollongong in Dubai (group 2, very good), and Sorbonne University-Abu Dhabi and Saint Joseph University-Dubai (group 3, good). The QS World University Rankings 2026 , and Arab university ranking (2024) have 12 public and private HE institutions but no foreign branch campus included. Negligible research impact “With the notable exception of NYU Abu Dhabi, which performs well on the Research Integrity Risk Index ( RI² ) and maintains a low research integrity-risk profile, most foreign branch campuses in the UAE, including those in Dubai, have had negligible research output or impact on the country’s academic landscape,” Meho noted. He said their primary focus has been on teaching and revenue generation rather than substantive research engagement. “This limited research activity constrains the applicability of RI² assessments to these institutions,” said Meho, who is the developer of the RI² – the world’s first empirically grounded, composite metric designed to identify and profile institutional-level risks to research integrity. “Whether the three newly announced campuses will follow the high-integrity, research-orientated model of NYU Abu Dhabi or align more closely with the largely teaching-focused profile of other foreign universities in the UAE remains to be seen.” Dubai’s foreign campuses are crucial to increasing access to higher education, particularly for its sizable and varied expatriate population, according to Meho. In addition, they minimise the financial and logistical burdens of studying abroad, promote global perspectives, and offer internationally accredited programmes – all of which should not be understated. “However, when it comes to research and innovation, that is, the core drivers of a true knowledge-based economy, their impact has been minimal. Despite the many foreign campuses in Dubai and the tens of thousands of students they enrol, they contribute to less than 25% of Dubai’s research output today,” Meho pointed out. “Realising Dubai’s D33 vision will ultimately require a shift toward deeper investment in research capacity, academic-industry linkages, and evidence-driven policymaking,” he concluded. Complex and uneven impact Rottleb is of the opinion that foreign campuses in Dubai promote knowledge-based economic development, but their impact is complex and uneven. “Branch campuses help Dubai strengthen its position as an emerging international education hub, diversifying transnational higher education beyond traditional Western centres. They meet demand for recognised degrees and supply skilled graduates to international companies operating locally,” he stated. “However, their contribution to building a truly local innovation ecosystem is limited.” He cautioned that even well-meaning institutions like KHDA, which genuinely seek to promote academic life and knowledge-based economy development, cannot fully overcome the boundaries set by the UAE’s authoritarian political climate, which restricts critical academic inquiry. Moreover, the majority of branch campus students – many of whom come from the resident migrant community in the United Arab Emirates – face residency insecurity and are focused on obtaining stable white-collar jobs or onward migration rather than long-term innovation-driven entrepreneurship. Research ambitions “Dubai’s model of hosting foreign universities in Free Zones has succeeded in attracting reputable global brands, including from non-Western countries. “But for branch campuses to move beyond being education service providers, there must be space for more open, critical academic engagement and attention to the social realities of the student population,” Rottleb pointed out. “While they supply qualified workers to international companies, genuine knowledge-based development also requires tackling the structural factors that currently limit local innovation capacity,” Rottleb suggested. For Rottleb, real knowledge-based development also requires tackling the structural factors that currently limit local innovation capacity, even as they supply qualified workers to international companies. Resultingly, branch campuses need to play a stronger role by being more integrated into local industry needs and national research priorities. “This means supporting joint research initiatives, incentivising collaboration with domestic universities, and investing in infrastructure for innovation. “Dubai also needs to offer incentives – particularly financial security – to encourage foreign universities to bring not only cash-cow teaching programmes but also research-intensive ones,” Rottleb explained. “Finally, attracting academics who conduct innovative research requires more than money: it demands creating an inspiring environment where people can think freely and critically engage with ideas,” he pointed out. Aligning branch and mother campuses Pacino argued that there could be stronger accreditation and quality assurances between foreign branches that (genuinely) align with mother campuses. In addition, there could be more promotion of regional partnerships with the industry’s bigger hitters, where they might create knowledge ecosystems to provide economic impacts such as workforce development and entrepreneurship. “Dubai’s strategic hub could benefit from a focus on policies that offer incentives to foreign campuses, not only to operate as a business, but to truly fulfil their customers’ (students’) needs with a holistic ecosystem that provides education and employment at the end of it,” Pacino said. Contributors to innovation For Meho, Dubai’s strategy to expand its higher education landscape through foreign branch campuses is commendable, particularly when it focuses on institutions that serve local needs while maintaining global standards. “However, for foreign campuses to truly add long-term value, Dubai must avoid becoming a haven for diploma mills or passive teaching outposts. The emphasis should be on establishing a reputation for academic integrity, research excellence, and societal and economic impact,” he cautioned. According to Meho, foreign branch campuses need to move beyond their current teaching-focused mandates and become active participants in the UAE’s research, innovation, and talent development ecosystems in order to better leverage branch campuses for economic development and fully align with Dubai's D33 and E33 agendas. A clear and intentional policy shift would be necessary for this transition, one that holds campuses accountable for their performance, promotes alignment with national strategic priorities, and incentivises meaningful research engagement. “Key recommendations include [adding] local relevance through mandating that branch campuses tailor academic programmes and research agendas to Dubai’s economic priorities, such as AI, healthcare, energy transition, and sustainability,” Meho suggested. Public-private partnerships through creating structured mechanisms for collaboration between campuses, industries, and government bodies to bridge the gap between education and workforce needs are also needed. In addition, accountability frameworks should be introduced that distinguish between teaching-only campuses and those contributing to knowledge production. Meho suggested that a shift of focus towards attracting research-intensive institutions, as Qatar did with Weill Cornell and Abu Dhabi did with NYU and Cleveland Clinic, is also needed. In order to raise branch campuses’ visibility and measure their influence, Meho proposed “ranking inclusion through advocating for the separate recognition and evaluation of branch campuses in regional and global university rankings”. He concluded: “Without such reforms, foreign campuses risk becoming passive educational outposts, but with them, they can become integral drivers of innovation, human capital development, and sustainable economic growth in Dubai.”

title: ‘Architect’ of flagship HE policy is nominated minister
content:
Tweet
The ‘architect’ of South Korea’s new president’s policy to have 10 major flagship universities in the country has been nominated as South Korea’s next minister of education under President Lee Jae-myung’s administration. Lee Jin-sook, former president of Chungnam National University, was nominated on 29 June.
Announcing the nomination, Chief Presidential Secretary Kang Hoon-sik said: “She was the first female president of Chungnam National University, her alma mater, and the first woman to lead a flagship national university in Korea.
She previously served as dean of the College of Engineering and as a member of the Presidential Advisory Council on Science and Technology.”
Lee chaired the policy team behind one of the president’s key campaign pledges: the ‘Ten Seoul National Universities’ initiative to upgrade ten universities around the country to the level of the country’s most prestigious institution, Seoul National University (SNU).
“She was recommended numerous times through the public nomination system,” Kang noted, referring to a system set up by President Lee Jae-Myung last month where citizens can directly propose candidates for major public office.
The ‘Ten Seoul National Universities’ policy was one of President Lee Jae-myung’s top ten pledges during his candidacy to replace impeached president Yoon Suk Yeol, who was removed after his declaration of martial law on 3 December 2024.
The flagship universities initiative proposes levelling up ten national universities across the country as a means to address educational inequality, ease university entrance pressures to get into the current few top universities in Seoul, and help reverse talent outflow from the regions.
“Support for flagship national universities will be expanded to a level comparable to SNU, allowing for the discovery of regional talent and enabling students to pursue master’s and doctoral degrees within their regions,” Lee said at a campaign rally in the southern city of Gwangju on 17 May.
The policy would involve a substantial boost in funding – particularly in per-student spending – and provision for collaboration with private universities and input from the education sector.
Currently, SNU spends about KRW60 million (US$43,800) per student, while those at other national universities receive just KRW25 million or less per student.
Lee’s education advisory team has proposed raising this amount to approximately 70% of the SNU level, according to party statements from 2024.
Chaired taskforce on flagship universities
Lee was officially appointed chair of the ‘Ten Seoul National Universities’ task force within the Democratic Party’s central campaign committee in May 2025, just before the election.
At a press briefing in Daejeon on 29 May, she explained: “The idea of ‘Ten Seoul National Universities’ has long been promoted by metropolitan and provincial superintendents (education officials), and when I suggested it to Lee Jae-myung’s campaign, it was enthusiastically adopted.
“It’s not just about creating elite regional universities – it’s about transforming the national education system and driving balanced development. I joined the campaign because I agreed with this vision.”
In 2020, Lee became the first woman in Chungnam National University’s 70-year history – and in any of Korea’s flagship national universities – to be elected president. Her election on 28 November 2019 was through a direct vote by faculty, students, and staff, reinforcing her democratic mandate. During her term, she pushed through academic reforms such as the establishment of a semiconductor-focused programme, laid the groundwork for a cross-regional campus model, and founded a new international studies division. A breach of this provision carries a maximum administrative fine of 1 million won. She only learnt of the issue recently and sincerely apologises to the public.” The spokesperson said: “All of the candidate’s publications between 2007 and 2019 were reviewed by Chungnam National University’s research ethics committee during her appointment process, and no misconduct was found.”

title: How do employers view the quality of HE and its graduates?
content:
Tweet
Employers considered the accreditation or recognition by a national professional body of an institution of higher learning, as well as its international ranking, as important factors in their decision-making about the employability of the institution’s graduates, a study in South Africa has revealed.
The study , captured in a recent report titled Stakeholder Perspectives on the Quality of Higher Education in South Africa, was prepared for the Council on Higher Education (CHE) by the South African Human Sciences Research Council.
The CHE publishes information about developments in higher education, including reports on the state of the sector, and promotes the access of students to higher education institutions, among other issues.
It aimed to investigate stakeholder perceptions of the quality of higher education. Overall, it surveyed three groups of participants: academic and management staff in public and private higher education institutions; current students and graduates; and private and public employers, employer organisations and external quality assurance bodies.
Employer sector
In the employer sector, 200 respondents from the government, community, social and personal services sectors were included. Also surveyed were those in the information and communications technology sphere; insurance, real estate and business services domain; and the manufacturing sector.
The largest proportion of respondents were human resources professionals, while there were several managers and senior professionals among the cohort.
“Performance of previous employees from that institution” was rated as important, although there was a greater spread in opinion in relation to this.
The study found that employer preferences “align with the … importance attached to compliance with norms and standards as a key measure of quality in higher education”.
What employers think about quality
The objective of the employer questionnaire was to determine what employers think is important for understanding and promoting quality in higher education. The survey questionnaire asked respondents to provide their views on higher education quality in relation to six composite measures:
•	Dimensions considered important for quality in higher education;
•	Graduate attributes to be developed through higher education;
•	Factors impacting on the decision to employ a graduate;
•	Important aspects of a university’s work in relation to its teaching, research and social responsibility functions;
•	Ways of assessing educational outcomes that are valued by employers; and •	Educational and recreational resources considered important for quality higher education. The institution you attend matters There was widespread agreement on the importance of the “institution that a graduate has attended” and the “reputation the institution has in South Africa among other employers”. External accreditation of the institution by international bodies was also important. The respondents unanimously acknowledged the importance of “socially and economically relevant and transformative” education as an indicator of quality with the importance of “personally transformative” education; education that is “accountable to stakeholders” and excellence and high standards in education, as other quality metrics. However, employers were comparatively less interested in value for money and appropriately resourced higher education as indicators of quality. Instead, they advised that higher education should focus on developing personal qualities in graduates such as self-esteem; personhood; recognition of the power of knowledge; self-discipline; and emotional stability and independence. The report indicated that employers “stressed the importance of developing cognitive and emotional attributes, including the capacity to reason and analytical skills”. There was also a sense that higher education should be making a social contribution; promote ethical awareness; and “produce graduates with a global perspective and a notion of citizenship”. Other institutional factors employers consider Other institutional factors that employers considered important in relation to employment decisions include institutional reputation in the context of histories of racism; sexual abuse or drug-related scandals and protests. “Staff achievements and the social contributions of institutions were also mentioned as critical factors,” according to the study. There was a high level of agreement on the importance of lecturers with teaching qualifications and lecturers who aim to transform attitudes and behaviours. There was more importance assigned by employers to lecturers having a teaching qualification as opposed to a PhD. “Employers clearly value lecturers’ exposure to pedagogy and content of the field they are teaching as opposed to a doctoral-level degree.” What about graduates’ grades? All those surveyed agreed on the importance of academic performance or high marks as a credible measure of assessing the outcomes of education, with 56.5% of participants rating this as “important” and 43.5% rating this as “very important”. There was also agreement on the importance of the other indicators for assessment. For example, continuous assessment to prepare students for their final assessments was rated as an effective way of measuring the quality of a graduate by 42.5% of the respondents. Similarly, “submission of documents, such as a CV and [a] qualification” was rated as important by 51% and as very important” by 42.5%. “There was an even greater unanimous acknowledgement of the importance of the indicator with the lowest mean score – assessment of academic knowledge – with 69.5% of respondents describing this indicator as important and the rest describing it as very important.” Educational resources and facilities Employers were asked to rate the importance of a number of educational and co-curricular resources and facilities as indicators of quality in higher education. The aspects which received the highest mean scores were financial support to students; cleanliness of campus and access to transport to and within the campus. The aspect which received the lowest mean score was student sports and sports facilities, even though most of the respondents rated the provision of such facilities as important. The respondents were less enthusiastic about the importance of student organisations and recreational facilities as an indicator of quality, although 60% noted that such provision was important. There was substantial agreement on the importance of a number of other educational and co-curricular resources and facilities as indicators of quality, including safety and security on campus; course materials and design; student instructional support; laboratories and other facilities; ICT, connectivity and computing and library resources. There was considerable agreement on the importance of online learning management systems; tutoring and small-group learning rooms; lecture halls; student health and psycho-social support; student residences; and number of students per class. “It is noteworthy that multilingualism was regarded as important by 54% of respondents and very important by 41%. While work experience from work-integrated learning, and job seeking and entrepreneurship skills were not selected by any employers as very important; the respondents generally viewed these attributes as either slightly important or important.” Positives and negatives In their consideration of various ways of measuring higher education outcomes, employers agreed unanimously on the importance of three main criteria: subject matter or academic knowledge; skills for the workplace and academic performance. Employers attached the greatest importance to knowledge and competence in the chosen degree or field of study. There was also almost unanimous support from employers for invigilated examinations as a test of knowledge and skills; alternative assessment methods (such as practicals and presentations) and continuous assessment. Employers indicated that “when hiring a graduate, the impression in a recruitment interview is more important than the grades”. The employer stakeholder group was critical about the (limited) extent of financial support (and the standard of the administration of funding) being offered to students; the quality of the social environment, social spaces and residences on campuses; the extent of the academic, counselling and mental health support provided to students; and the responsiveness of institutional governance processes in addressing student grievances. The stakeholders were generally positive in their assessment of change in the quality of higher education in democratic South Africa with respect to equity, expansion, diversity, and inclusion in higher education; the quality of academic staff and the involvement of academic staff in quality assurance, the study indicated. The employer stakeholder group recommended the fostering of collaboration between higher education institutions and employers, private industry and state-owned enterprises, local communities, community-based organisations and government and public entities, to align educational provision with societal and economic needs. The establishment of partnerships to support student skills development through initiatives such as industry placements, work-integrated learning, practicals, internships, and business incubation centres was also recommended.

title: When openness obscures power – Rethinking MOOCs
content:
Tweet
In the global rush to digitise learning, the word ‘open’ has become synonymous with progress. But not all openness is created equal.
Massive open online courses (MOOCs) have been celebrated as democratising forces, breaking down educational barriers and expanding access worldwide. Yet beneath the appealing rhetoric lies a more complex and more troubling reality.
MOOCs are not the same as open-access learning. They are platformised, proprietary, and often aligned more with profit than pedagogy.
The mirage of MOOC openness
When MOOCs were launched in the early 2010s by institutions like Stanford, MIT, and Harvard, they promised a revolution in global education.
Platforms like Coursera, edX, and FutureLearn offered free courses from top-tier universities, using the language of access, inclusion, and global empowerment. Millions enrolled, governments signed on, and the hype cycle surged.
But the model evolved rapidly into a commercial ecosystem. Courses became ‘freemium’, certificates came with a cost, and platform algorithms optimised engagement for monetisation.
A 2024 study published in Open Praxis analysed MOOCs on the Bilge portal and also noted persistently low completion rates, even after adjusting for engagement. This contextualises past findings and confirms that dropout remains a core issue in MOOCs.
Another study examined 2.3 million learners across 174 MITx courses, Open Praxis . The authors concluded that MOOCs continue to attract learners who are disproportionately older, male, and highly educated, indicating that those who least need open access education often benefit most.
Platform capitalism and data extraction
Today’s MOOCs operate under the logic of platform capitalism. Their governance is centralised, their content is institutionally curated, and their design prioritises scalability and data-driven personalisation over critical engagement.
Behavioural data is mined to enhance stickiness and convert users into paying customers, echoing the broader patterns of surveillance capitalism .
MOOCs promise global learning but often deliver digital franchising. The platforms act more like SaaS (Software-as-a-Service) companies than educational commons.
The knowledge offered is typically Western, English-language, and linear, with limited adaptability for local contexts. Instead of transforming learning, they simulate the traditional classroom on a digital interface.
MOOCs export knowledge – But seldom import context
MOOCs frequently export Western knowledge without meaningful local context, reinforcing patterns of digital neocolonialism. Their epistemic orientation favours Anglo-American paradigms, reinforcing a form of digital neocolonialism. Scholars such as Walter Mignolo have called this the “coloniality of knowledge”.
Courses on global development, education, or health are frequently written from elite Global North perspectives, with minimal representation of Global South voices or Indigenous knowledge systems. As a result, learners are socialised into accepting one way of knowing, while local traditions are sidelined or omitted entirely. Language is another barrier. Over 80% of MOOCs are offered in English , excluding millions of learners across the Global South who lack high-level proficiency. Even in multilingual initiatives like SWAYAM (India) or FUN MOOC (France), the pedagogy often mirrors colonial-era models – top-down, exam-driven, and institutionally guarded. What true open access learning looks like In contrast to MOOCs, open-access learning emphasises community, flexibility, and cultural relevance. Rooted in the tradition of knowledge commons, it is marked by community-led curriculum design, multilingual resources, open licensing, and peer-to-peer pedagogy. It values learner agency over credential scalability. Consider: The African Storybook Project : enables communities to develop and translate children’s books into local languages. Refugee-led coding academies in Lebanon : teaching Python through oral storytelling, blending tech with cultural narratives. Latin American women’s cooperatives : developing digital literacy tools from the ground up. These are not MOOCs. They are not massive. But they are open in the deepest sense: participatory, situated, and emancipatory. Case studies from four continents National MOOC platforms across the globe have adopted distinct strategies to expand access and assert cultural influence. While they differ in form and intention, a common thread runs through their designs: each platform reflects not only a pedagogical model but also a political project – embedding specific values, epistemologies, and power relations into digital learning. FutureLearn (United Kingdom): Cultural diplomacy through MOOCs Founded by the Open University and supported by the United Kingdom government, FutureLearn has actively positioned itself as a soft power instrument . Its initiatives include offering free courses to Afghan women and Ukrainian students during moments of political crisis, framed explicitly as part of broader public diplomacy efforts. These efforts extend Britain’s historical educational outreach, particularly in regions with colonial-era ties. UK universities partner through the platform to deliver English-language instruction and cultural curricula, reinforcing British influence under the banner of inclusion and humanitarian support. While access is broadened, the epistemic orientation remains largely Anglocentric. SWAYAM (India): Infrastructure without pedagogical transformation India’s SWAYAM platform (Study Webs of Active Learning for Young Aspiring Minds) was launched by the Ministry of Education to provide free, multilingual online courses from Indian universities. It represents a commendable effort to build national digital infrastructure and reduce dependency on foreign edtech platforms. However, SWAYAM’s pedagogy remains deeply traditional, lecture-based, exam-driven, and focused on institutional authority. While it expands access, the platform’s hidden curriculum emphasises standardised success and individual merit, often marginalising critical pedagogy, learner agency, and cultural plurality. As a result, SWAYAM preserves rather than transforms prevailing educational hierarchies. FUN MOOC (France): Linguistic sovereignty and neo-republican education Launched in 2013 by the French Ministry of Higher Education, France Université Numérique ( FUN MOOC ) explicitly promotes Francophone education as a form of global cultural outreach. The platform has deepened ties with former French colonies, particularly through the Francophonie agenda – such as initiatives ahead of the 2024 Villers Cotterêts Summit , and by rolling out localised versions in countries like Morocco and Côte d’Ivoire. Though its pedagogy often mirrors the centralised, lecture-heavy model of France’s higher education system, FUN MOOC carries a clear decolonising impulse: it prioritises linguistic sovereignty and cultural continuity in the Francophone world. Yet, it stops short of embracing participatory learning or epistemic plurality, reflecting a neo-republican model of top-down educational dissemination. Coursera and edX (United States): Market logics and the coloniality of knowledge US-based MOOC platforms like Coursera and edX (now part of 2U) commercialise elite education at scale, distributing content from institutions such as Stanford and MIT to a global audience. Backed by Silicon Valley and academic prestige, they promote a hidden curriculum rooted in neoliberal values – self-optimisation, market alignment, and entrepreneurialism. Learners are framed as individual upskillers in gamified environments, with critical inquiry sidelined. Most content reflects Anglo-American epistemologies, often excluding Global South or Indigenous perspectives. This reinforces what decolonial scholars call the coloniality of knowledge, where power over learning remains concentrated in the Global North. The hidden curriculum: What MOOCs really teach The case studies above illuminate a deeper structural tension: while national MOOC initiatives have succeeded in broadening access and localising content to varying degrees, their true impact hinges less on technical infrastructure and more on the degree of epistemic autonomy they afford. The central question is not merely what MOOCs deliver, but how they structure the act of learning itself. Beneath the surface of open access lies a hidden curriculum, one that transmits the cultural logics of self-optimisation, competition, and credentialism. Learning is reframed as a solitary race toward certification, gamified into metrics and milestones. Reflection gives way to retention; transformation is replaced by task completion. Dialogue, where it exists, is constrained, funnelled through algorithmically managed forums that reward speed and superficiality over sustained inquiry. In this design, it is not the learner’s context, culture, or curiosity that shapes the learning journey; it is the logic of the platform. Algorithmic personalisation, standardised templates, and institutional branding dictate not only what is taught, but also how, why, and to whom. The result is a pedagogy of scale; that is, broad in reach but often shallow in depth, optimised for distribution, not for discovery. This is the paradox of MOOCs: they democratise access to elite content while centralising control over knowledge production. What appears open may, in practice, reinforce old hierarchies, just dressed in the aesthetics of innovation. Toward a participatory, equitable future To move beyond this constrained model, we must reimagine digital education as a relational and co-created space – one that values learning as a public good, not a product. That means shifting the paradigm from passive consumption to active participation. True openness in education requires: • Funding public, open-source digital infrastructure, including community-managed servers, multilingual content repositories, and low-bandwidth tools that serve under-connected regions. • Supporting culturally embedded content creation by local educators, using inclusive pedagogical frameworks that reflect linguistic and epistemic diversity. • Prioritising learner-led initiatives, such as peer learning networks, open badges, collaborative curriculum design, and grassroots knowledge hubs. • Embedding ethical frameworks in edtech design that centre equity, pluralism, and collective care rather than metrics and monetisation. Openness must move beyond technical access or enrolment figures. If it is to be liberatory, it must be rooted in agency, context and shared authorship. Otherwise, we risk confusing digital scale for educational justice. Conclusion: Reclaiming the meaning of openness MOOCs are not inherently harmful – but they are not inherently emancipatory either. Too often, they deliver accessibility without equity, scalability without cultural sensitivity, and instruction without participation. In doing so, they risk deepening the very inequalities they claim to address. Reclaiming openness means recentring education around human relationships, between teacher and learner, and between communities and knowledge systems. It means designing platforms that are accountable not just to venture capital or institutional prestige, but to the plural and evolving needs of learners worldwide. The mirage of MOOC openness
When MOOCs were launched in the early 2010s by institutions like Stanford, MIT, and Harvard, they promised a revolution in global education.
Platforms like Coursera, edX, and FutureLearn offered free courses from top-tier universities, using the language of access, inclusion, and global empowerment. Millions enrolled, governments signed on, and the hype cycle surged.

A 2024 study published in Open Praxis analysed MOOCs on the Bilge portal and also noted persistently low completion rates, even after adjusting for engagement. This contextualises past findings and confirms that dropout remains a core issue in MOOCs.
Another study examined 2.3 million learners across 174 MITx courses, Open Praxis . The authors concluded that MOOCs continue to attract learners who are disproportionately older, male, and highly educated, indicating that those who least need open access education often benefit most.
Platform capitalism and data extraction
Today’s MOOCs operate under the logic of platform capitalism. Their governance is centralised, their content is institutionally curated, and their design prioritises scalability and data-driven personalisation over critical engagement.
Behavioural data is mined to enhance stickiness and convert users into paying customers, echoing the broader patterns of surveillance capitalism .
MOOCs promise global learning but often deliver digital franchising. The platforms act more like SaaS (Software-as-a-Service) companies than educational commons.
